Paper title: Reinforcement Learning for Option Hedging: Static Implied-Volatility Fit versus Shortfall-Aware Performance
Overview: This paper addresses the decoupling between pricing-model calibration and real-world hedging performance by shifting the hedging objective from traditional error-minimization to shortfall-probability optimization. The authors extend the QLBS framework by operationalizing its computational stage and embedding shortfall probability into its reward structure, and introduce a novel RLOP (Replication Learning of Option Pricing) model. They compare these RL approaches against Black-Scholes, Merton jump-diffusion, and Heston stochastic volatility baselines using SPY and XOP call options data from 2020Q1 (COVID crash) and 2025Q2.
Technology stack: ResNet-style network (He et al. 2016) for policy and value networks, REINFORCE with baseline, Adam optimizer at learning rate 10⁻⁴. Simulated environment generates GBM price paths.
Improvements: Extends QLBS by operationalizing its computational stage, embedding shortfall probability into reward, and introducing diminishing factor d_T(t) and replacing variance with square root for numerical stability. RLOP introduces reward shaping via stacking ensemble of maturities for intermediate feedback.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Extends QLBS framework by operationalizing its latter computational stage and embedding shortfall probability into reward structure; (2) Introduces novel RLOP model for tail-risk resilience and computational efficiency; (3) Offers selection framework through bidirectional computational architecture where backward-operating QLBS acts as cost-aware stabilizer and forward-calculating RLOP serves capital-constrained desks.
Methodology: Two RL paradigms: (1) Adaptive QLBS—backward value-based approach with value function V_t^π(X_t) = E_t^π[-d_T(t)Π_t(X_t) - λΣγ^(T-t)√Var[Π_t(X_t)]], modified with diminishing factor and square root of variance; (2) RLOP—forward replication learning where agent manages portfolios Π_t^(i) for expiries i=1,...,T, choosing hedge positions u_t^(i) for all t<i, with reward R_t = H(h(S_t),Π_t^(i)) where H(x,y) = -|x-y| or squared variant. Policy parametrized as Gaussian π = N(μ_π,σ_π) with shared ResNet-style network.
Limitations on the work: The numerical scheme is restricted to trades of exactly ±Δy shares per step in SC. The paper notes divergence between SC and DH prices at high transaction costs. DH networks trained on finite batches may not adequately price extreme scenarios. SC scheme uses binomial tree while DH uses Monte Carlo, producing systematically different estimates. No code availability stated.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: SPY and XOP call options from two non-overlapping quarters: 2020Q1 (COVID crash, high-volatility regime) and 2025Q2 (calmer regime). Daily snapshots from DoltHub repository post-no-preference/options. Contracts with 3 to 70 calendar days to maturity, focusing on 28-day bucket.
Evaluation Metric Used: IVRMSE, Hedging RMSE, Average trading cost, Shortfall probability
keywords: Option hedging, reinforcement learning, QLBS, shortfall probability, transaction costs, risk aversion, implied volatility, stochastic volatility.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides framework for embedding shortfall probability into RL reward structure. Demonstrates how to compare RL-based hedging against parametric benchmarks under transaction costs. Offers evaluation methodology using multiple metrics.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it explores RL-based hedging under transaction costs and compares against parametric baselines including Heston, which matches my simulated market setup. It provides a framework for evaluating hedging performance using multiple metrics (RMSE, trading cost, shortfall probability) that I can adopt. The modified QLBS and RLOP architectures demonstrate how to embed risk measures like shortfall probability into the reward structure, which is directly relevant to my CVaR-based objective. However, it does not use learned representations like JEPA or autoencoders—the state is the normalized price X_t and time. I can use this paper as a baseline methodology for deep hedging under transaction costs and as a source for evaluation metrics, but the representation learning component is absent.
Challenges: Computational complexity, path-dependent instruments, funding-spread jumps, and model risk noted as future work. Discretization error in SC scheme. Finite batch training for DH may miss extreme scenarios.
Key Proofs: Proposition 1 with proof in Appendix B: For sufficiently large ε in the linear transaction cost assumption TC(Δu,S) = ε|Δu|S, the option price C(S₀) is monotonically increasing in both λ (risk aversion) and ε (transaction cost).

Paper title: DeltaHedge: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portfolio Options Optimization
Overview: This paper presents DeltaHedge, a multi-agent framework integrating options trading with AI-driven portfolio management. It coordinates specialized agents for forecasting, sentiment analysis, trading, and dynamic hedging under a central mechanism. The system employs an ensemble strategy for hedging, training multiple RL agents (PPO, DDPG, A2C) concurrently and selecting the best performer quarterly. Experiments on S&P 500, Apple, and Tesla demonstrate outperformance over traditional strategies and standalone models.
Technology stack: Stable-Baselines3 for RL models (PPO, DQN, A2C, DDPG) trained for 20,000 timesteps. Informer (transformer-based) for forecasting. DistilRoBERTa-financial-sentiment for sentiment analysis. PyTorch implied. Hardware not stated. Code not stated.
Improvements: First multi-agent framework integrating options-based hedging with equity trading. Ensemble strategy dynamically selects best RL algorithm quarterly. Cross-attention mechanism for inter-agent communication. Integration of sentiment analysis and forecasting for market regime detection.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Introduces DeltaHedge, novel multi-agent framework integrating options-based hedging into equity trading workflows; (2) Proposes ensemble-based hedging strategy dynamically selecting among multiple RL agents; (3) Presents comprehensive benchmarking and ablation study evaluating against traditional methods, standalone RL baselines, and LLM-based frameworks.
Methodology: Hierarchical multi-agent system with Coordinator Agent, Forecasting Agent (Informer), Sentiment Analysis Agent (DistilRoBERTa), Trading Agent (PPO), and Hedging Agent (ensemble of PPO/A2C/DDPG). Shared reward based on Sharpe ratio change: R_t = SR_t - SR_{t-1}. Cross-attention for inter-agent communication. Quarterly retraining with 90-day lookback and 30-day validation. Leverage constraints on hedging positions.
Limitations on the work: System exclusively engages in long positions, excluding short selling. Protective options incorporated strictly for downside risk mitigation. Daily data used since most market crashes occur overnight. The ensemble's advantage over best single hedger is small in some cases (5 basis points Sharpe for Apple). Classic delta hedge performs poorly on Apple but well on Tesla.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Stock price data: S&P 500, Apple, Tesla from Yahoo Finance. Options data: optionsdx.com. Sentiment data: EOD Historical Data. VIX from Yahoo Finance. Training period: Jan 2010-Dec 2019 (S&P 500), Jan 2016-Dec 2019 (AAPL, TSLA). Testing: Jan 2020-Dec 2024.
Evaluation Metric Used: Sharpe Ratio, Sortino Ratio, Calmar Ratio, Total Return, Maximum Drawdown, Volatility
keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Multi-Agent Systems, Portfolio Management, Options Trading, Deep Reinforcement Learning.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides evaluation metrics and ablation methodology. Demonstrates ensemble strategy for RL hedging. Shows how to integrate options into portfolio management.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is tangentially relevant because it involves options hedging with RL, but it focuses on portfolio-level management with equity and protective puts rather than deep hedging of a single option with a learned representation. The state includes OHLCV data, sentiment scores, and VIX, but no learned embeddings. The ensemble strategy for hedging is interesting but not directly applicable to my JEPA representation learning focus. I can use the evaluation metrics (Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, MDD) and the ablation study methodology, but the multi-agent architecture is more complex than needed for my single-option hedging experiment.
Challenges: Ensemble advantage small in some cases. Classic delta hedge performs poorly on some assets. Quarterly retraining adds computational cost.
Key Proofs: None stated.

Paper title: Bridging Stochastic Control and Deep Hedging: Structural Priors for No-Transaction Band Networks
Overview: This paper studies hedging and pricing of a European call option under proportional transaction costs from two perspectives: stochastic control (CARA utility, HJBQVI, Whalley-Wilmott asymptotic approximation) and deep hedging (two architectures building on No-Transaction Band Network: NTBN-Δ and WW-NTBN). The WW-NTBN incorporates the Whalley-Wilmott formula as a structural prior on bandwidth and replaces hard clamp with differentiable soft clamp. Numerical experiments show WW-NTBN converges faster, matches stochastic control bands more closely, and generalizes well across transaction cost regimes. The framework is also applied to bull call spread.
Technology stack: Feedforward neural networks with 5 hidden layers of 32 units each, ReLU activations. Adam optimizer with learning rate 10⁻². Monte Carlo simulation for GBM paths. Binomial tree for stochastic control. No code availability stated.
Improvements: NTBN-Δ formalizes delta-centring as explicit design choice with theoretical justification. WW-NTBN incorporates Whalley-Wilmott formula as structural prior, providing correct scaling with λ and γ at initialization. Soft clamp replaces hard clamp, providing non-zero gradients everywhere. Faster convergence and better generalization across transaction cost regimes.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Unified theoretical exposition of optimal hedging under proportional transaction costs following Davis et al. (1993) with CARA utility; (2) NTBN-Δ: makes delta-centring explicit with theoretical justification; (3) WW-NTBN: incorporates Whalley-Wilmott formula as structural prior and replaces hard clamp with differentiable soft clamp; (4) Comprehensive numerical comparison across models and transaction cost levels; (5) Application to bull call spread documenting breakdown of price linearity.
Methodology: Stochastic control: HJBQVI with CARA utility, dimension reduction, Whalley-Wilmott asymptotic band. Deep hedging: MLP baseline, NTBN-Δ (delta-centred band with learned half-widths), WW-NTBN (WW prior + residual correction, soft clamp). Training: minimize entropic risk measure ρ_γ(X) = (1/γ)log E[e^{-γX}]. Indifference pricing via (63). Bull call spread: joint vs naive hedging.
Limitations on the work: WW-NTBN partly sacrifices model-agnostic character of deep hedging by incorporating Black-Scholes delta and gamma as structural inputs, implicitly assuming log-normal dynamics. SC scheme restricted to trades of exactly ±Δy shares per step. DH networks trained on finite batches may not fully reflect rare extreme scenarios. Gap between SC and DH prices at high transaction costs from compounding factors.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated GBM paths. Parameters: S₀=K=1.0, σ=0.2, r=μ=0, γ=1.0, T=1.0. Transaction costs: λ ∈ {0%, 0.1%, 0.5%, 1%, 5%}. For bull call spread: K₁=0.9, K₂=1.1.
Evaluation Metric Used: Option prices (writer and buyer indifference prices), No-transaction band geometry, Terminal P&L distributions, CVaR (95%), Trade frequency, Average shares traded, Entropic training loss
keywords: Stochastic control, Deep Learning, Option Hedging, Transaction costs, No-transaction band, Whalley-Wilmott.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides WW-NTBN architecture with structural prior for transaction cost settings. Offers comparison methodology between SC and DH. Demonstrates importance of structural priors for convergence and generalization.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it directly addresses the integration of structural priors into deep hedging architectures, which is analogous to my interest in using JEPA-learned representations as a structural prior. The Whalley-Wilmott formula as a structural prior is conceptually similar to how I might use a learned representation to inform the hedging policy. The paper provides rigorous methodology for comparing deep hedging against stochastic control solutions, which I can adapt for comparing JEPA-based representations against oracle and baseline representations. The no-transaction band architecture is directly applicable to my transaction cost setting. However, the paper does not use representation learning—it uses hand-crafted features (log-moneyness, time to maturity, volatility) and Black-Scholes Greeks. I can use the WW-NTBN as a baseline architecture and the comparison methodology (band geometry, P&L distributions, trade metrics) for my experiments.
Challenges: WW-NTBN assumes log-normal dynamics. SC numerical scheme has discretization error. DH networks may miss rare extreme scenarios. Gap between SC and DH prices at high transaction costs.
Key Proofs: Proposition 2.3 (Dimension reduction under CARA utility): Under CARA utility, value function takes form U(t,S,y,X) = 1 - e^{-γX/δ(t,T)}Q(t,y,S), eliminating cash dimension. Proof in Appendix A. Theorem 1: Existence of unique finite solution for Deep Bellman Hedging equation. Proof via Banach fixed-point theorem. Theorem 2 (Vanilla Deep Hedging Bellman Equation). Theorem 3: Existence of finite unique solutions for Vanilla Deep Hedging Bellman Equation. Sketch of Whalley-Wilmott asymptotic derivation in Appendix B.

Paper title: Application of Deep Reinforcement Learning to At-the-Money S&P 500 Options Hedging
Overview: This paper applies deep Q-learning to hedging at-the-money S&P 500 index options using a Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) agent. The agent is trained on historical intraday prices from 2004-2024 using a single continuous time series of six predictor variables. A walk-forward procedure provides nearly 17 years of out-of-sample evaluation. The DRL agent is benchmarked against Black-Scholes delta hedging. Results show the DRL agent outperforms delta hedging, particularly in volatile or high-cost environments, though performance deteriorates with higher risk-aversion parameters.
Technology stack: PyTorch for TD3 implementation. Actor: 2 hidden layers of 256 with LeakyReLU (negative slope 0.05), Tanh output. Critics: 3 hidden layers of 256, LeakyReLU (0.05), linear output. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck exploration noise with decay. Replay buffer capacity 10000. Code available at https://github.com/zof-br/DRL_hedging.
Improvements: Uses single continuous time series instead of segmented episodes (Mikkila and Kanniainen 2023). Extensive 17-year out-of-sample evaluation. Sensitivity analysis across transaction costs, volatility windows, and risk penalty parameters.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Novel approach using single continuous time series of at-the-money S&P 500 call options without careful path selection; (2) Demonstrates superiority of DRL over delta hedging across different trading cost levels and risk aversion; (3) Provides extensive out-of-sample evaluation over 17 years.
Methodology: Finite-horizon MDP with TD3 agent. State: 6-dimensional vector (option price, underlying price, time-to-maturity, moneyness, realized volatility, current hedge position). Action: new hedge ratio clipped to [-1,1]. Reward: R_t = PnL_t - ξ|PnL_t| where PnL_t = HO_t(C_t - C_{t-1}) + HS_{t-1}(S_t - S_{t-1}) - c|S_t||ΔHS_t|. Walk-forward training with hyperparameter tuning each window.
Limitations on the work: DRL model sensitive to environment parameters. Performance deteriorates with higher risk-aversion parameter. Negative returns in base case despite outperforming benchmark. Number of parameters to tune makes it difficult to reach full potential. Margin requirements not accounted for. High drawdowns observed.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Historical prices of at-the-money call options on S&P 500 with 30-day maturity and S&P 500 itself from 2004-2024. Source: CBOE DataShop. 30-minute frequency for rebalancing. Training: walk-forward approach. Testing: 17 years out-of-sample.
Evaluation Metric Used: Cumulative PnL, Annualized return (ARC), Annualized Std. dev. (ASD), Sharpe Ratio, Information Ratio, Adjusted Information Ratio, Max Drawdown (MDD), Final PnL (%)
keywords: Deep learning, Reinforcement learning, Double Deep Q-networks, options market, options hedging, deep hedging.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides detailed TD3 implementation for option hedging. Offers hyperparameter ranges and walk-forward methodology. Demonstrates sensitivity analysis for transaction costs, volatility windows, and risk penalty.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it provides a detailed empirical implementation of deep hedging using TD3 on real S&P 500 options data with transaction costs and risk-awareness penalties. The state space includes realized volatility, which is one of my baseline representations. The walk-forward methodology and hyperparameter tuning approach are directly applicable to my experiment design. However, the paper does not use learned representations (no autoencoders, no JEPA)—it uses hand-crafted features. I can use this paper as a benchmark for TD3-based deep hedging and as a source for hyperparameter ranges and evaluation metrics. The finding that longer volatility windows produce more stable results is relevant to my realized-volatility baseline.
Challenges: DRL sensitivity to environment parameters. High drawdowns. Negative returns in some scenarios. Computational cost of hyperparameter tuning each window.
Key Proofs: None stated.

Paper title: Learning to Hedge Swaptions
Overview: This paper investigates deep hedging for dynamic hedging of swaptions, contrasting with traditional sensitivity-based rho-hedging. The authors design agents under three objective functions (MSE, downside risk, CVaR) and evaluate how these objectives shape hedging styles. Using a three-factor arbitrage-free dynamic Nelson-Siegel model for simulation, they find that near-optimal hedging effectiveness is achieved with two swaps as hedging instruments. Deep hedging strategies dynamically adapt exposure to risk factors across market states and outperform rho-hedging even under model misspecification.
Technology stack: PyTorch for automatic differentiation. shap package for feature importance. KAN (Kolmogorov-Arnold Network) with RBF kernels for pricing. Code available on GitHub (not specified). Adam optimizer with learning rate 5×10⁻³.
Improvements: First deep hedging application to swaptions using DTAFNS model. Uses portfolio value as state variable (not used by benchmarks). Compares three objective functions and their hedging styles. Residual sensitivity analysis to understand risk exposures.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) First application of deep hedging to swaptions (except Oya 2024) using DTAFNS model; (2) Demonstrates how different risk preferences (MSE, DR, CVaR) translate into distinct hedging styles; (3) Evaluates marginal value of additional hedging swaps; (4) Shows robustness to model misspecification; (5) Uses KAN for swaption pricing and sensitivity computation.
Methodology: Deep hedging with FCNN: 4-layer network with hidden layer widths [8, 32, 32, 8], Mish activation, linear output. Input: Y_t = (X_t, T_α-t, V_t). Three objectives: MSE, DR (downside risk), CVaR. Training: 100,000 Monte Carlo paths, batch size 2048, Adam optimizer, 800 epochs max, early stopping patience 200. Leverage bounds imposed post-hoc via projection. KAN for swaption pricing: 3 layers with widths [8, 16, 8], RBF kernels, trained on 20,000 paths.
Limitations on the work: No closed-form solution for swaption price—uses KAN approximation. Leverage constraints imposed post-hoc rather than during training. Model misspecification tests limited to perturbations of κᴾ and θᴾ. Swaption prices and sensitivities computed via neural network approximation.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated data using DTAFNS model calibrated on end-of-month Canadian spot rate curves from January 1986 to January 2022 (434 months). ATM swaption with maturity T_α = 60 months, 5y×10y payer swap, fixed rate K = 2.5083%. Hedging portfolio rebalanced monthly.
Evaluation Metric Used: Mean, RMSE, Root Downside Risk (RDR), CVaR₉₉%, P(HE>0), Hedging Risk Reduction (HRR), Trading Intensity (TI), Dynamic Tracking Error (DTE)
keywords: Swaptions, Dynamic Hedging, Deep Reinforcement Learning, Term Structure Models, Risk Management.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides methodology for comparing different risk objectives in deep hedging. Demonstrates feature importance analysis using SHAP. Offers evaluation metrics (RDR, HRR, TI, DTE). Shows robustness to model misspecification.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is tangentially relevant because it applies deep hedging to a different asset class (swaptions) and uses a different market model (DTAFNS). However, the methodology for comparing different risk objectives (MSE, downside risk, CVaR) is directly applicable to my CVaR-based objective. The finding that portfolio value as state variable contributes to outperformance is relevant to my state representation design. The use of KAN for pricing approximation is interesting but not directly applicable to my Heston simulation setup. I can use the evaluation metrics (RDR, HRR, TI, DTE) and the residual sensitivity analysis methodology.
Challenges: No closed-form swaption price. Leverage constraints imposed post-hoc. Model misspecification limited to parameter perturbations. Computational cost of KAN training.
Key Proofs: None stated.

Paper title: Data-driven Derivative Hedging with Quadratic Variation Penalty
Overview: This paper considers hedging a European call option under discrete rebalancing with transaction costs. The authors formulate a stochastic optimal control problem maximizing hedge P&L with quadratic variation of P&L as a penalty term. They solve numerically using deep stochastic optimal control (deepSOC) and deep reinforcement learning (deepRL) under Black-Scholes and SABR models. Under Black-Scholes, they show delta hedging is not optimal when penalized for quadratic variation. Results show data-driven methods outperform delta hedging when accounting for transaction costs and pathwise variability.
Technology stack: DeepSOC: 30 feedforward neural networks trained independently with Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.01) for 200 epochs, each with 50,000 samples. Networks: 3 layers with widths [10, 15, 10], batch normalization. DeepRL: PPO with actor-critic, 2 layers with width 10 each. Optuna framework for hyperparameter optimization. PyTorch implied.
Improvements: Introduces quadratic variation penalty on P&L as objective. Shows delta hedging non-optimality under this objective. Compares deepSOC and deepRL approaches. Tests under both Black-Scholes and SABR models.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Proposes objective function with quadratic variation penalty on P&L, incorporating accumulated variability into hedging strategy; (2) Shows delta hedging is not optimal under quadratic variation penalty even in Black-Scholes; (3) Compares deepSOC and deepRL approaches for dynamic hedging; (4) Tests under both Black-Scholes and SABR models.
Methodology: Stochastic optimal control: maximize E[V_T - (λ/2)⟨V⟩_T] where ⟨V⟩_T is quadratic variation of P&L. Discretized objective: J_Π = E[Σ(P&L_t - (λ/2)P&L_t²)]. deepSOC: trajectory optimization with neural network policy, 30 independent networks, Adam optimizer. deepRL: PPO with actor-critic, GAE parameter τ=0.98, discount γ=0.95, clip ε=0.2, c1=0.5, c2=0.0001. Market models: Black-Scholes and SABR.
Limitations on the work: DeepRL with PPO shows larger variance in performance than deepSOC. Occasional out-of-sample underperformance with long right tail. DeepSOC can produce outliers due to noisy training process. No margin requirements considered. Limited to single option hedging.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated data. Black-Scholes: μ=5%, σ=20%. SABR: σ=20%, η=0.5, ρ=0.6. Spot price $100, strike $100, maturity 30 days. Risk-free rate r=0. Transaction cost κ=0.001. Daily rebalancing.
Evaluation Metric Used: Hedge P&L, Quadratic variation of P&L, Empirical P&L densities
keywords: Derivative Hedging, Stochastic Optimal Control, Deep Learning, Trajectory Optimization, Reinforcement Learning.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides quadratic variation penalty formulation. Compares deepSOC and deepRL. Shows non-optimality of delta hedging under pathwise variability. Offers training details for both approaches.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it formulates hedging as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic variation penalty, which is related to my CVaR/risk-measure objective. The comparison between deepSOC and deepRL provides insights into different training paradigms. The finding that delta hedging is not optimal under pathwise variability penalties is relevant to my evaluation of representations. The paper uses simulated Black-Scholes and SABR models, which are related to my Heston setup. I can use the quadratic variation penalty formulation and the comparison methodology. However, the paper does not use learned representations—the state is the raw price path. The deepSOC approach with trajectory optimization is different from my policy-based RL approach.
Challenges: DeepRL variance larger than deepSOC. Outliers in out-of-sample performance. No margin requirements. Limited to single option.
Key Proofs: Section 2.3: Non-optimality of BS delta-hedge with quadratic variation penalty. First-order condition gives optimal strategy H_t* = Δ_t^BS + (1/λS_t)(μ/σ²), showing correction term proportional to Sharpe ratio. No formal theorem/proof number, but derivation provided.

Paper title: Data-driven Hedging with Generative Models
Overview: This paper proposes a nonparametric data-driven methodology for hedging using generative models. A conditional generative model trained on market data simulates realistic market scenarios given current conditions, and hedge ratios are computed to minimize risk across scenarios. The approach incorporates transaction costs, enables optimal selection of hedging instruments, and adapts to market conditions. The method is illustrated for hedging option portfolios using VolGAN, a generative model for implied volatility surfaces. Out-of-sample performance matches and improves over delta and delta-vega hedging without retraining for more than 4 years.
Technology stack: VolGAN (generative model for implied volatility surfaces). LASSO regression with coordinate descent. Python (shap package mentioned). Code available at https://github.com/milenavuletic/VolGAN/.
Improvements: Uses generative model for scenario generation instead of parametric model. Incorporates transaction costs via ℓ₁ penalty leading to sparsity. Automatic selection of hedging instruments. No retraining needed for over 4 years. Forward-looking scenarios instead of backward induction.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Proposes nonparametric data-driven methodology using conditional generative models for hedging; (2) Uses conditional variance minimization leading to linear hedge ratios computable via linear regression; (3) Incorporates transaction costs via ℓ₁ penalty leading to LASSO regression and automatic hedging instrument selection; (4) Demonstrates effectiveness for hedging volatility risk using VolGAN; (5) Shows out-of-sample performance without retraining for over 4 years.
Methodology: Conditional generative model G generates one-step-ahead scenarios (S_{t+Δt}, X_{t+Δt}) given current market conditions. Hedge ratios computed by solving LASSO regression: min_{A_t,φ_t} (1/N)Σ(ΔV_t(ω_k) - A_t - Σφ_t^iΔH_t^i(ω_k))² + αg₀Σc_t^i|φ_t^i - φ_{t-Δt}^i|. Coordinate descent with soft thresholding. VolGAN for implied volatility surface generation. Delta-vega hedging benchmark.
Limitations on the work: Conditional variance minimization limited to linear hedge ratios. Assumes stationarity. Generative model may not capture regime changes. Market impact model uses linear assumption.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: SPX options from OptionMetrics, January 2000 - February 28, 2023. Training: January 3, 2000 - June 16, 2018. Testing: subsequent period. Long straddle portfolio with strikes K = m₀S₀ for m₀ ∈ {0.75, 0.8, 0.9, 1.1, 1.2, 1.25}. 52 non-overlapping one-month periods.
Evaluation Metric Used: Tracking error statistics: Mean, Median, Standard Deviation, Value-at-Risk (5%, 2.5%, 1%). Number of hedging instruments selected. Delta and vega statistics.
keywords: Data-driven hedging, Generative models, GAN, Implied volatility surfaces, Transaction costs, LASSO regression.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides methodology for data-driven hedging using generative models. Offers automatic hedging instrument selection via LASSO. Demonstrates long-term out-of-sample performance. Provides comparison with delta-vega hedging.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it uses generative models to simulate market scenarios for hedging, which is conceptually related to my use of JEPA to learn a representation of price history. The conditional variance minimization approach is different from my CVaR objective, but the LASSO regression for automatic instrument selection is interesting. The paper demonstrates that data-driven hedging can outperform model-based approaches without retraining for extended periods. However, the paper does not use RL—it uses direct optimization via regression. The generative model (VolGAN) is used for scenario generation, not representation learning. I can use the evaluation methodology (tracking error statistics, VaR) and the comparison with delta-vega hedging.
Challenges: Conditional variance minimization limited to linear hedge ratios. Assumes stationarity. Generative model may not capture regime changes. Market impact model uses linear assumption.
Key Proofs: Proposition 2.2: Hedge ratios minimizing conditional variance of tracking error are given as regression coefficients of ΔV_t on {ΔH_t^i}. Proof provided. Remark 2.3 discusses self-financing condition. Remark 2.5 expresses minimization as regression of values rather than changes.

Paper title: Deep Bellman Hedging
Overview: This paper discusses an actor-critic-type reinforcement learning algorithm for hedging a portfolio of financial instruments using purely historic data. The approach solves a Bellman equation for the optimal value function where the operator U represents a risk-adjusted return metric. Key characteristics include: ability to hedge with derivatives, incorporation of trading frictions, applicability to any reasonable portfolio, realistic continuous state and action spaces, and formal risk-adjusted return objectives. The trained model provides optimal hedge for arbitrary initial portfolios and market states without retraining. The paper proves existence of finite solutions to the Bellman equation and shows relation to vanilla Deep Hedging.
Technology stack: TensorFlow or PyTorch mentioned for solving interpolation problem. No specific implementation details. No code availability stated.
Improvements: Extends Deep Hedging to dynamic programming version. Provides optimal hedge for arbitrary initial portfolios without retraining. Does not impose boundary condition on future maturity. Uses monetary utilities for well-posed Bellman equation. Finite Markov Representation for portfolios. Proves existence of unique finite solutions.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Presents practical implementation for solving Bellman equation with risk-adjusted return metric; (2) Extends Deep Hedging to dynamic programming version that provides optimal hedge for arbitrary initial portfolios without retraining; (3) Provides numerical implementation method for representing arbitrary portfolios as states using purely historic data; (4) Clarifies conditions under which Bellman equations are well-posed and admit unique finite solutions; (5) Proves existence of unique finite solution for Deep Bellman Hedging equation.
Methodology: Deep Bellman Hedging: find value function V* satisfying V*(z;m) = sup_a U[β(m)V*(z' + a·h';M') + R(a;z,m,M')|m]. Actor-critic algorithm: (1) Actor: find optimal policy π^(n) maximizing expression; (2) Critic: estimate new value function V^(n) via interpolation. Monetary utilities: normalized, monotone increasing, concave, cash-invariant. Finite Markov Representation (FMR): represent instruments by feature vectors (book value, greeks, scenarios). Randomly sample portfolios and market states for training.
Limitations on the work: Model limited by coverage of historic scenarios used to train it. Human oversight still required for abrupt changes in market scenarios. Assumes every hedging instrument has time-to-maturity less than τ* (excludes perpetual assets). The choice of Q (probability distribution over portfolio and market states) is non-trivial. No empirical validation.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Historic market data (not specified). No empirical experiments. Theoretical paper with numerical implementation method.
Evaluation Metric Used: Not stated (no empirical results).
keywords: Deep hedging, Bellman equation, Reinforcement learning, Actor-critic, Monetary utility, Portfolio management.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides theoretical foundation for Bellman-based deep hedging. Offers Finite Markov Representation for portfolios. Proves existence of unique finite solutions. Enables hedging of arbitrary portfolios without retraining.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it provides the theoretical foundation for Bellman-based deep hedging that can handle arbitrary portfolios and market states without retraining. The concept of Finite Markov Representation (FMR) for portfolios is directly related to my interest in learned representations of price history. The paper's approach to representing portfolios as states using historic data (greeks, scenarios, etc.) is conceptually similar to how I might use a JEPA-learned representation as a state. The Bellman equation formulation with monetary utilities and the proof of existence of unique finite solutions provide rigorous theoretical grounding. I can use the FMR concept to design my state representation and the Bellman equation framework to formulate my hedging problem. However, the paper does not use JEPA or any specific representation learning method—it uses hand-crafted features (greeks, scenarios). I can use this as a theoretical foundation and extend it with learned representations.
Challenges: Choice of Q (distribution over portfolio and market states) is non-trivial. Model limited by historic scenario coverage. Excludes perpetual assets. No empirical validation.
Key Proofs: Theorem 1: Existence of unique finite solution for Deep Bellman Hedging equation. Proof via Banach fixed-point theorem (page 15). Theorem 2: Vanilla Deep Hedging Bellman Equation (page 14). Theorem 3: Existence of finite unique solutions for Vanilla Deep Hedging Bellman Equation (page 14). Proposition 1: If market has only finite statistical arbitrage, then U[G^π(z)] ≤ E[G^0(z)] + γ < ∞ (page 13). Corollary 1: Cash value function U* is only a solution to Deep Bellman Hedging problem if U = E (page 14).

Paper title: Pricing and Hedging Autocallable Products by Markov Chain Approximation
Overview: This paper proposes a unified pricing framework based on continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) approximation for autocallable structured products with all major features including autocall, snowball effect, and down-and-out American barrier. The authors derive pricing recursions over different monitoring dates computed using matrix exponentiation under CTMC approximation. They also propose a hybrid Markov chain approximation method for stochastic local volatility (SLV) models and introduce a systematic approach to improve dynamic hedging of autocallables in the presence of transaction costs using barrier shifting and payoff modification methods, with CVaR minimization via stochastic gradient descent.
Technology stack: MATLAB on workstation with Intel Xeon CPU E5-2687W and 64GB memory. Matrix exponentiation with scaling and squaring algorithm. Stochastic gradient descent with mini-batches. No code availability stated.
Improvements: First unified pricing framework for autocallables with all major features. Hybrid Markov chain method significantly improves computational efficiency over CKN. First systematic approach to determine optimal size of barrier shifting and payoff modification for CVaR minimization.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) General computationally efficient pricing method for autocallables applicable to broad range of models (jumps, regime-switching, local/stochastic volatility, time dependence); (2) Hybrid Markov chain approximation for SLV models that improves original two-layer CTMC algorithm; (3) Systematic approach to improve dynamic hedging using barrier shifting and payoff modification with CVaR minimization via SGD.
Methodology: CTMC approximation: construct continuous-time discrete state Markov process to approximate original continuous state process. Pricing recursions using matrix exponentiation. Grid design with piecewise uniform structure satisfying conditions from Zhang and Li (2019). Hybrid Markov chain for SLV: approximate variance process using discrete time Markov chain (DTMC) and adjust grid for transformed asset price. Dynamic hedging: delta hedging with barrier shifting and payoff modification, CVaR minimization via SGD.
Limitations on the work: Grid design requires careful implementation to achieve second-order convergence. For VG model, convergence is approximately 1.5 order. Hybrid scheme introduces time discretization error. Optimization problem only needs to be solved at inception but requires pricing and delta calculation at each rebalancing date. The paper does not consider margin requirements.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated data. Models: BS, RSBS, TIBS, CEV, Kou, VG, SABR, Heston. Autocallable I: 4-year contract with S₀=100, n=4, h=1, D=100, U=115, C=90, B=75, H=80, y=8%, z=5%. Autocallable II: 3-year ELS with S₀=100, n=6, h=0.5, D=(95,95,95,90,90,90), B=55.
Evaluation Metric Used: IVRMSE, absolute error, relative error, computation time. CVaR at 5% and 1% significance levels, maximum drawdown, Sharpe ratio, Calmar ratio.
keywords: Autocallable products, structured products, Markov chain approximation, CTMC, stochastic local volatility, dynamic hedging, CVaR, transaction costs.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides CVaR minimization via SGD for determining optimal barrier shifting and payoff modification. Offers grid design principles for CTMC approximation. Demonstrates hybrid Markov chain method for SLV models.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it addresses dynamic hedging with CVaR minimization using stochastic gradient descent, which is directly applicable to my CVaR-based objective. The barrier shifting and payoff modification techniques for managing delta explosion near barriers are interesting but specific to autocallables. The CTMC approximation method is not directly applicable to my Heston simulation setup, but the general framework for CVaR minimization via SGD is relevant. I can use the CVaR minimization formulation and the barrier shifting/payoff modification concept if I encounter similar delta instability issues. The paper does not use learned representations—it uses model-based pricing.
Challenges: Grid design for multiple barriers with discontinuities. Time discretization error in hybrid scheme. Optimization requires pricing and delta calculation at each rebalancing date. Limited to single asset autocallables.
Key Proofs: Proposition 1 (page 18): Convergence of hybrid scheme to two-layer CTMC as K→∞. Proof in Appendix B. Proposition 2.3 (page 11): Dimension reduction under CARA utility. Grid design conditions from Zhang and Li (2019) for second-order convergence.

Paper title: Hazard-Gated Temporal Transformers for Real-Time Risk Control
Overview: This paper proposes HedgeFormer, a hazard-gated temporal transformer that jointly models (i) time until next high-volatility event, (ii) cross-sectional location where risk concentrates, and (iii) corresponding action intensity. The model integrates survival-style temporal point-process heads with a multi-horizon hedging policy, enabling actions to be activated only when forecasted risk exceeds execution costs. Evaluated on short-dated cryptocurrency options, HedgeFormer significantly improves Sharpe, reduces CVaR₀.₉₉, and lowers turnover relative to delta-based methods, sequence-model hedgers, and Hawkes- or RL-driven timers.
Technology stack: 4-layer causal transformer (hidden size 256, 8 heads, GELU activations) with learned relative positional encodings. AdamW optimizer (learning rate 10⁻⁴, cosine decay, gradient clipping at 1.0). Walk-forward training with 12 months training, 3 months validation, 3 months testing.
Improvements: First to couple event-time prediction with cost-aware actions in a unified architecture. Hazard gating reduces turnover while improving tail-risk control. Factorized spatio-temporal design improves calibration and interpretability.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Hazard-gated temporal transformer coupling event-time prediction with cost-aware actions; (2) Factorized spatio-temporal design improving calibration and interpretability under bursty dynamics; (3) Reproducible evaluation demonstrating advantages over reactive policies.
Methodology: HedgeFormer: spatio-temporal transformer backbone with three heads: (1) Time head: log-normal distribution for inter-arrival time to next high-impact event, trained via negative log-likelihood; (2) Cross-sectional head: softmax for strike-tenor bucket allocation; (3) Multi-horizon action head: MLPs for hedge ratios at 1m, 5m, 30m horizons. Hazard-gated execution: γ_t = σ((z_t - τ_ha)/β), h̃_t = (1-γ_t)h_{t-} + γ_tδ_t. Training objective: L = L_time + L_back + λ_share L_share + μ_cvar CVaR₀.₉₉ + ηE[C(Δh)].
Limitations on the work: Execution model is simplified. Framework primarily targets delta risk. Extensions to richer cost dynamics, multi-Greek hedging, and robustness under structural regime shifts are future work. The model uses a deadband that suppresses micro-adjustments.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Deribit public WebSocket API: BTC and ETH short-dated European options (0DTE/1DTE), January 2021 - June 2025. Control grid: 1-minute. Features: ΔIV, imbalance, 1-min log returns, funding, volatility proxies, time encoding, bucket index. Burst labeling: 5-min realized variance exceeding rolling 95th percentile of trailing 30-day distribution.
Evaluation Metric Used: Annualized Sharpe ratio, Cumulative PnL (USD thousands), CVaR₀.₉₉ (USD tail loss), Turnover (bps of notional), Calibration metrics (PIT histograms and reliability curves)
keywords: Hazard-gated temporal transformer, event-timed decision making, survival analysis, temporal point processes, cryptocurrency options, risk control.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides hazard-gated execution policy for timing hedging actions. Offers calibration metrics (PIT histograms, reliability curves). Demonstrates walk-forward evaluation protocol. Provides architecture for combining timing, allocation, and action intensity.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it addresses the timing of hedging actions based on predicted risk, which is conceptually related to my use of JEPA to learn a representation of price history that can inform hedging decisions. The hazard-gated execution policy—activating actions only when predicted instability is high—is analogous to using a learned representation to gate hedging actions. The architecture combines survival analysis, cross-sectional allocation, and multi-horizon actions, which provides a template for integrating learned representations into a hedging policy. However, the paper does not use JEPA—it uses a temporal transformer with hazard gating. I can use the hazard-gated execution concept and the evaluation metrics (Sharpe, CVaR, turnover) for my experiments. The paper also demonstrates the importance of calibration for timing decisions.
Challenges: Simplified execution model. Primarily targets delta risk. Computational cost of transformer with attention. Data availability from Deribit.
Key Proofs: None stated.

Paper title: A Topological Approach to Parameterizing Deep Hedging Networks
Overview: This paper shows that by adding topological features (persistence diagrams, L¹/L² norms) to deep hedging networks, batch sizes can be reduced substantially without greatly compromising hedging performance. The authors evaluate four models (with/without topological features, batch sizes 20 and 1000) on a cliquet option under Heston model, demonstrating that topological features reduce PnL variance and enable smaller batch sizes to achieve similar results.
Technology stack: First layer: dense layers of dimension 32 with TanH activation. Four stacked LSTM cells of dimension 32. Final dense layer with dimension 1. Loss: scaled PnL variance (γ=1000). Trained for ~5300 epochs. PyTorch implied.
Improvements: First to use topological features for deep hedging. Demonstrates 10x reduction in batch size requirements. Shows that topological features lead to more meaningful hedges.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Introduces topological features (L¹/L² norms of persistence diagrams) to deep hedging; (2) Demonstrates that topological features reduce batch size requirements by 10x; (3) Shows that topological features lead to more meaningful hedges (lower PnL variance despite larger trades).
Methodology: Feature set: spot price S_t, realized volatility v_t, cliquet payout ψ_t, and L¹/L² norms of these features in rolling window size 15. Topological features: Vietoris-Rips complex R(X,ε), persistence diagrams for 0-dimensional homology, L¹/L² norms. Network: dense layers (dim 32) + 4 LSTM cells (dim 32) + dense output (dim 1). Loss: γ∇[Ω(T) - ψ(x,T)] where Ω(T) is PnL, γ=1000. Cliquet payoff: ψ(x,t) = max[Σ min(x_i/x_{i-1}-1, μ), 0] with cap μ=0.035.
Limitations on the work: Only tested on cliquet option under Heston model. Batch sizes limited to 20 and 1000. No transaction costs considered. Moving window size fixed at 15. Topological features add computational overhead. No comparison with other representation learning methods.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated Heston model: dS_t = μS_t dt + √v_t S_t dW_t^S, dv_t = κ(θ-v_t)dt + ξ√v_t dW_t^v. Parameters: μ=0.02, v₀=0.025, κ=2.5, θ=0.02, ξ=0.6, ρ=-0.5. 240 time steps. Cliquet cap μ=0.035. 50,000 test paths.
Evaluation Metric Used: PnL standard deviation, PnL skewness, average trade size, tail-risk PnL outcomes.
keywords: Deep hedging, topological data analysis, persistence diagrams, cliquet options, Heston model, recurrent neural networks.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides topological features for state representation. Demonstrates batch size reduction. Offers evaluation methodology (PnL variance, tail-risk outcomes). Shows that representation matters for hedging performance.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it introduces topological features as a form of state representation for deep hedging, which is conceptually related to my use of JEPA to learn a representation of price history. The L¹/L² norms of persistence diagrams capture structure in the data that can inform hedging decisions. The finding that topological features enable smaller batch sizes is interesting for training efficiency. However, the paper does not use JEPA—it uses hand-crafted topological features. I can use the topological features as an additional baseline representation and the evaluation methodology (PnL variance, tail-risk outcomes) for my experiments. The paper also demonstrates the importance of representation for hedging performance.
Challenges: Computational overhead of topological features. Limited to cliquet option and Heston model. No transaction costs. Moving window size fixed. Batch sizes limited.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses Vietoris-Rips complex and persistence diagrams from topological data analysis.

Paper title: Enhancing Deep Hedging of Options with Implied Volatility Surface Feedback Information
Overview: This paper presents a dynamic hedging scheme for S&P 500 options where rebalancing decisions are enhanced by integrating information about the implied volatility surface dynamics. The optimal hedging strategy is obtained through a deep policy gradient-type reinforcement learning algorithm. The favorable inclusion of forward-looking information embedded in the volatility surface allows the procedure to outperform several conventional benchmarks such as practitioner and smiled-implied delta hedging procedures in simulation and backtesting experiments, with outperformance more pronounced in the presence of transaction costs.
Technology stack: RNN-FNN architecture: 2 LSTM cells (width 56), 2 FFNN hidden layers (width 56) with ReLU, output layer with leverage constraint. TensorFlow, Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.0005), dropout p=0.5. Trained on 400,000 paths, tested on 100,000 paths.
Improvements: First to incorporate IV surface information directly as state variables in multi-stage RL-based hedging. Introduces leverage constraint to prevent doubling strategies. Demonstrates that IV surface information is critical for RL hedging to outperform benchmarks.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) First to conduct multi-stage RL-based hedging that incorporates IV surface information directly as state variables; (2) Uses JIVR model of François et al. (2023) for joint dynamics of underlying and IV surface; (3) Demonstrates that IV surface information is critical for RL hedging to outperform benchmarks; (4) Introduces leverage constraint to prevent doubling strategies; (5) Global importance analysis of IV surface factors using SAGE.
Methodology: Deep hedging with RNN-FNN architecture. State spaces: full (V_t, δ_t, τ_t, S_t, {β_t,i}, h_t,R, {h_t,i}), reduced with δ_t (δ_t, τ_t, S_t, {β_t,i}, h_t,R), reduced without δ_t (τ_t, S_t, {β_t,i}, h_t,R). Penalty functions: MSE, SMSE, CVaR₉₅%, CVaR₉₉%. Leverage constraint: B_t(Z) = min(Z, B_t). JIVR model for market dynamics. Training: mini-batch SGD with Adam.
Limitations on the work: Focuses on hedging with underlying asset only (no options as hedging instruments). Uses simulated data from JIVR model for training. State space reduction may lose some information. Leverage constraint B=100. Dropout parameter p=0.5. No closed-form solution for swaption pricing.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated data from JIVR model estimated on S&P 500 data from January 4, 1996 to December 31, 2020. Backtesting: December 31, 2020 to October 31, 2023, 4,134 around-the-money call options. No transaction costs in main experiments (κ=0), with transaction costs κ ∈ {0.05%, 0.5%, 1%}.
Evaluation Metric Used: Avg P&L, CVaR₉₅%, CVaR₉₉%, MSE, SMSE, CVaR deviation, hedging costs.
keywords: Deep reinforcement learning, optimal hedging, implied volatility surfaces, JIVR model, CVaR, transaction costs.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides RNN-FNN architecture for deep hedging. Offers SAGE analysis for feature importance. Demonstrates state space reduction. Provides leverage constraint formulation. Uses JIVR model for realistic market dynamics.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it demonstrates the importance of state representation for deep hedging—specifically, that including forward-looking IV surface information significantly improves hedging performance. This directly supports my hypothesis that a JEPA-learned representation of price history can improve hedging. The paper provides a methodology for evaluating feature importance (SAGE) and a state space reduction approach that I can adapt. The RNN-FNN architecture is similar to what I might use. The finding that portfolio value can be omitted from the state space is relevant for my state design. I can use the IV surface factors as a baseline representation and the SAGE analysis to compare with my JEPA representation. The paper also demonstrates that RL hedging can outperform delta hedging when given the right information.
Challenges: Computational cost of training on 400,000 paths. State space selection requires experimentation. Leverage constraint B=100. JIVR model estimation requires 25 years of data. No options as hedging instruments.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses SAGE (Shapley Additive Global Importance) for feature importance.

Paper title: Adaptive-QLBS and RLOP: Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Option Hedging
Overview: This paper introduces two RL frameworks: a novel Replication Learning of Option Pricing (RLOP) approach and an adaptive extension of Q-Learner in Black-Scholes (QLBS), forming an end-to-end, friction-aware pricing and hedging pipeline. Both methods use risk-sensitive replication objectives as proxies for downside-sensitive hedging under transaction costs. The models are tested on realized pathwise delta-hedging outcomes, shortfall probability, and tail-risk measures using listed SPY and XOP options. RLOP reduces shortfall frequency across most regimes and achieves the strongest tail-risk improvements under stress, while implied-volatility fit often favors parametric models yet fails to predict after-cost hedging performance.
Technology stack: ResNet with D stacked residual blocks (D ∈ {2,3,4}), 9-dimensional input, embedded coordinate transforms, Gaussian policy with sigmoid-clamped std, REINFORCE with baseline, Adam optimizer (lr 10⁻⁴), PyTorch, N_par = 2,500 parallel paths, two-mode inference (GPU training/CPU inference).
Improvements: Extends QLBS with downside-sensitive risk-adjusted replication objectives. Introduces RLOP with 3-network decoupled design (policy, value, PriceEstimator). Embeds differentiable analytical layer for end-to-end training with interpretable implied-volatility representation. Risk-cost maps separate replication quality from execution costs.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Extends QLBS framework by incorporating downside-sensitive, risk-adjusted replication objectives into reward structure, resolving decoupling between static calibration and execution; (2) Introduces novel RLOP model as forward replication-learning approach for tail-risk-sensitive hedging; (3) Provides selection framework supported by risk-cost maps and downside-risk analysis; (4) Introduces differentiable analytical layer embedding closed-form pricing formula within neural computation graph; (5) Three-network decoupled design for RLOP with dedicated PriceEstimator.
Methodology: Adaptive-QLBS: backward value-based RL with modified value function V_t^π(X_t) = E_t^π[-d_T(t)Π_t - λΣγ^{τ-t}√VarΠ_τ], where d_T(t) = (1-t/T) is diminishing factor and variance is square-rooted for numerical stability. RLOP: forward replication learning with ensemble of maturities, agent manages portfolios Π_t^(i) for expiries i=1,...,T, reward R_i = H(h(S_i),Π_i^(i)) where H penalizes replication error. 3-network design: policy π_θ, value baseline V_φ, PriceEstimator P_ψ. Differentiable analytical layer: network outputs latent volatility σ̂, passed into closed-form pricing formula P (Black-76) implemented as differentiable PyTorch module.
Limitations on the work: IVRMSE is not a reliable proxy for hedging quality. RL policies not designed as IV interpolators. Limited to European call options on SPY and XOP. Training on simulated paths may not fully capture market dynamics. No code availability.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: SPY and XOP European-style call options across two quarters: 2020Q1 (COVID dislocation) and 2025Q2 (calmer conditions). Daily option snapshots, maturities grouped into buckets centered at τ ∈ {28, 56} days. Moneyness K/F. Calibration uses same-day option cross-section. RL models pretrained on simulated paths (GBM).
Evaluation Metric Used: Expected Shortfall (ES₅%, ES₁₀%), shortfall probability P(PnL_T^net < 0), RMSE(ξ_T), average trading cost E[TC_T], IVRMSE.
keywords: Option pricing, Reinforcement learning, Dynamic hedging, Shortfall risk, Deep Neural Network, QLBS, RLOP.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides differentiable analytical layer for embedding closed-form pricing in neural network. Offers 3-network decoupled design for RLOP. Risk-cost map evaluation methodology separates replication from execution. ES and shortfall probability metrics for tail-risk evaluation.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it directly addresses the same core problem I am investigating: the disconnect between pricing calibration and hedging performance, and the use of RL with risk-sensitive objectives. The differentiable analytical layer is conceptually similar to embedding a learned representation (like JEPA) within the policy network. The three-network decoupled design (policy, value, PriceEstimator) provides an architectural template I can adapt. The risk-cost map evaluation methodology is directly applicable to my experiments. The findings on IVRMSE vs. hedging performance support my motivation that representation learning (rather than just calibration) matters. The paper does not use JEPA—it uses a differentiable pricing layer—but the architectural principle of embedding structural knowledge is analogous. I can use the risk-cost map, the ES metrics, and the shortfall probability as evaluation metrics. The 3-network design with PriceEstimator is an interesting alternative to standard actor-critic.
Challenges: IVRMSE is not a reliable proxy for hedging quality. RL policies not designed as IV interpolators. Limited to European call options on SPY and XOP. Training on simulated paths may not fully capture market dynamics. No code availability.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses differentiable analytical layer (closed-form pricing formula) as inductive bias.

Paper title: Black-Scholes Meet Imitation Learning: Evidence From Deep Hedging in China
Overview: This paper introduces an imitation learning deep hedging (ILDH) algorithm that bridges the Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) model with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to address option hedging in incomplete real markets. The DRL agent optimizes its hedging policy using both freely explored action samples based on real trading data and corresponding action demonstrations derived from the BSM model. These demonstrations serve as data augmentation, enabling the agent to develop a meaningful policy even with a relatively small training data set and enhancing management of tail risk. Empirical results show ILDH achieves higher profit, lower risk, and lower cost in the Chinese stock index options market compared to other deep hedging algorithms and traditional delta hedging.
Technology stack: RNN-TD3: TD3 (Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient) with RNN layers. Actor network π(o_t, h_t^l), Critic networks Q_j(o_t, a_t, h_t^l) for j=1,2. RNN structure for historical information. DAgger algorithm for imitation learning. Named algorithms: TD3, DDPG, DQN, DAgger, BSM delta hedging.
Improvements: First to combine imitation learning with deep hedging for option hedging. Uses BSM model as expert for demonstrations, addressing limited data and tail risk. Models option hedging as POMDP with RNN memory structure. Demonstrates superior performance in Chinese market with limited data (3 years).
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Introduces ILDH algorithm combining imitation learning (DAgger) with TD3 for option hedging; (2) Uses BSM model as "expert" to provide demonstrations, addressing limited real trading samples and tail risk problems; (3) Models option hedging as POMDP rather than MDP and integrates RNN structure into TD3; (4) Demonstrates superior performance in Chinese CSI 300 stock index options market.
Methodology: ILDH: TD3 algorithm as core, DAgger imitation learning module with BSM as expert, RNN memory structure. State: moneyness (K/S_t), TTM, implied volatility, current holding, option price. Action: number of units of underlying asset n_t. Reward: r_{t+1} = PnL_t - ξ|PnL_t| with terminal reward including E(PnL) - ξ·SD(PnL). Training: precompute BSM demonstrations, store in replay buffer, DAgger combines agent exploration samples with BSM demonstrations. POMDP formulation with memory h_t^l = o_{t-l}, a_{t-l+1}, ..., o_t, a_{t-1}. RNN-TD3: Critic Q(o_t, a_t, h_t^l), Actor π(o_t, h_t^l).
Limitations on the work: Dataset spans 3 years of trading data—may not capture all market regimes. Only tested on CSI 300 stock index options. Limited news data for training. Limited access to open interest contracts. The model relies on BSM demonstrations which may be less relevant in extreme market conditions not represented in training data. No code availability (available upon request).
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: CSI 300 stock index options, 30-min high-frequency data, 3 years of trading data. Call option training set: 3,352 episodes, test: 1,678. Put option training set: 3,466, test: 1,699. Each episode: 1 week (5 trading days), 8 hedging steps per day (30-min), 40 steps per episode. Moneyness 0.9 ≤ K/S_0 ≤ 1.1, TTM 10-60 trading days.
Evaluation Metric Used: Reward, P&L, Cost, Std P&L, VaR (95%), CVaR (95%).
keywords: Deep reinforcement learning, imitation learning, option hedging, TD3, POMDP, Chinese market.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides imitation learning framework for deep hedging with limited data. Offers POMDP formulation with RNN memory structure. DAgger algorithm for combining expert demonstrations with exploration. Ablation study methodology. RNN-TD3 architecture.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it uses imitation learning to bridge theoretical models (BSM) with DRL, which is conceptually similar to using a JEPA-learned representation as a "prior" for hedging. The DAgger algorithm combining expert demonstrations with exploration samples is analogous to how I might use JEPA representations alongside raw features. The POMDP formulation and RNN memory structure are directly relevant to my state representation design—the paper shows that historical information matters for hedging. The ablation study methodology (comparing with/without memory and imitation learning) is directly applicable to my experiments. However, the paper does not use JEPA—it uses BSM demonstrations. I can use the POMDP formulation, the RNN-TD3 architecture, and the ablation methodology. The finding that imitation learning improves tail risk management is relevant to my CVaR objective.
Challenges: Limited real trading data (3 years). BSM demonstrations may be less relevant in extreme market conditions. Limited news data for training. No access to open interest contracts. Model may need retraining for different markets.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses DAgger algorithm from Ross et al. (2011).

Paper title: Distributional Adversarial Attacks and Training in Deep Hedging
Overview: This paper studies the robustness of classical deep hedging strategies under distributional shifts by leveraging the concept of adversarial attacks. The authors demonstrate that standard deep hedging models are highly vulnerable to small perturbations in the input distribution, resulting in significant performance degradation. Motivated by this, they propose an adversarial training framework tailored to increase robustness of deep hedging strategies. The approach extends pointwise adversarial attacks to the distributional setting and introduces a computationally tractable reformulation of the adversarial optimization problem over a Wasserstein ball, enabling efficient training of hedging strategies resilient to distributional perturbations. Extensive numerical experiments show adversarially trained strategies consistently outperform classical counterparts in out-of-sample performance and resilience to model misspecification, maintaining reliable performance on real market data and during periods of market change.
Technology stack: Neural network: two hidden layers, each with 20 neurons, batch normalization, ReLU activation. Architecture consistent with standard deep hedging [2]. Named algorithms: FGSM, PGD, WPGD, WBPGD, Adam optimizer, distributionally robust optimization. Code available in supplemental material.
Improvements: First unified framework for distributional adversarial training in deep hedging. Tractable reformulation of adversarial optimization over Wasserstein ball for deep hedging. Demonstrates improved out-of-sample and out-of-distribution performance with limited data. Validates on real market data and compares against robust deep hedging approach.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) First framework unifying distributional adversarial training with deep hedging; (2) Derives computationally efficient adversarial attacks within a Wasserstein ball and integrates them into adversarial training; (3) Empirically demonstrates adversarially trained strategies outperform classical deep hedging in out-of-sample and out-of-distribution performance with limited data (5,000-100,000 samples); (4) Validates framework on real market data, demonstrating robustness during market stress.
Methodology: Deep hedging framework: minimizes risk measure ρ[PnL(θ,I)]. OCE risk measures: ρ(Z) = inf_ω {ω + E[ℓ(-Z-ω)]}. DRO formulation: min_θ max_{η∈B_δ(μ)} E_{η}[l_DH(θ,I)]. Pointwise adversarial attacks: FGSM, PGD. Distributional adversarial attacks: maximize expected loss over Wasserstein ball. Theorem 3.3 provides tractable approximation. WPGD (Wasserstein Projection Gradient Descent) and WBPGD (Wasserstein Budget Projection Gradient Descent) algorithms. Adversarial training: L_adv(θ) = αΣl_DH(θ;X_n) + Σl_DH(θ;X̂_n). Heston extension: S-Attack (perturb price only) and SV-Attack (perturb both price and variance).
Limitations on the work: Performance remains sensitive to choice of Wasserstein radius δ, which may differ across models. The adversarial training introduces additional computational cost (approximately 10x for BS model, 10x for Heston model). The approach assumes Lipschitz continuity of loss function. The study does not compare with other RL methods besides deep hedging. No experiments on historical data following original DH methodology.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: Black-Scholes, Heston, General Affine Diffusion (GAD). Training: 100,000 sample paths, partitioned into subsets of 5,000-100,000. Test: 1 million paths. OOD: 100 perturbed parameter configurations (±10% scaling), 1 million paths. Real data: S&P 500 companies (AAPL, AMZN, BRK-B, GOOGL, MSFT) from 26 Sep 2008 to 8 Mar 2020. FIX dataset: GAD model with fixed parameters from 250-day period. ROBUST dataset: GAD model with parameter robustness.
Evaluation Metric Used: Hedging loss (entropic risk, CVaR), out-of-sample performance, out-of-distribution performance, Frobenius distance between covariance matrices, autocorrelation function (ACF) differences, P&L on real data.
keywords: Deep hedging, adversarial attacks, distributionally robust optimization, Wasserstein distance, model misspecification, robustness.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides tractable framework for distributional adversarial training in deep hedging. Offers WPGD and WBPGD algorithms for generating adversarial distributions. Paper title: Deep Hedging Under Non-Convexity: Limitations and a Case for AlphaZero
Overview: This paper provides a mathematical analysis of the limitations of Deep Hedging (DH), demonstrating its close relationship with traditional convex optimization. The authors show that in settings where utility is concave and increasing and transaction costs are convex, portfolio replication becomes a convex problem in the space of deterministic policies, explaining why DH performs well. When DH is applied to non-convex environments (e.g., non-convex transaction costs, liquidity constraints), it fails with non-negligible probability. The authors propose an alternative RL-based approach inspired by Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and AlphaZero/MuZero, showing these methods consistently identify optimal courses of action where DH fails and require fewer training samples.
Technology stack: DH: stack of shallow NNs, recurrent NN, or LSTM. AlphaZero: MCTS with NNs for policy and value, UCB1, self-play training. MuZero: learned dynamics model, representation function, prediction function. Network architectures: four hidden layers with 256 or 512 neurons, batch normalization, ReLU, tanh output for value, softmax for policy. Adam optimizer (lr 0.001). Optuna for hyperparameter optimization. Hardware: Intel Core i5-12600K, 32GB DDR5, NVIDIA RTX 3090.
Improvements: First mathematical analysis of DH limitations in non-convex environments. Proof that DH converges to local optima in non-convex settings. Proposal of AlphaZero/MuZero as alternative that consistently identifies optimal strategies. Demonstration of improved sample efficiency with MCTS-based methods.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Mathematical analysis of DH limitations, showing close relationship with convex optimization; (2) Proof that under concave increasing utility and convex costs, portfolio replication is convex in policy space, explaining DH success; (3) Demonstration that DH fails in non-convex environments (multimodal Q*, disconnected domains); (4) Proposal of AlphaZero/MuZero-based approach that consistently identifies optimal replication strategies where DH fails; (5) Demonstration of improved sample efficiency with MCTS-based methods.
Methodology: Portfolio replication as MDP: state S_k = (t_k, δ_k, X_k, p_0 + Π_k + Σc_j), action A_k = δ_{k+1}^{1:m}, reward at maturity = u(PL_n). DH: stack of NNs or recurrent NN, deterministic policy, end-to-end training via gradient descent. AlphaZero: MCTS with UCB1, NN for policy and value, self-play training. MuZero: learned dynamics model, planning in latent space. Theoretical analysis: convexity of Q* under concave increasing utility and convex costs. Counterexamples: quadratic utility (non-increasing), non-convex costs, cash constraints. Experiments: minimal environments with multi-modal rewards, toy market models with non-concave Q*, GBM market with non-convex costs, trinomial market with trading constraints, sample efficiency comparison.
Limitations on the work: AlphaZero's high infrastructure complexity. Scalability in high-dimensional asset spaces. Limited to toy examples and simulated markets. No historical data experiments. Comparison only with DH.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: Black-Scholes, Heston, trinomial market, GBM. No historical data. Toy examples with discrete states and actions. Cliquet option (mentioned in related work).
Evaluation Metric Used: Hedging loss (mean-squared loss), terminal P&L, frequency of correct actions, sample efficiency (number of training samples).
keywords: Deep Hedging, Reinforcement Learning, Monte Carlo Tree Search, AlphaZero, MuZero, Non-Convex Optimization, Portfolio Replication.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides theoretical framework for understanding DH limitations. Offers AlphaZero/MuZero as alternative for non-convex environments. Demonstrates sample efficiency improvements. Game-theoretic interpretation of replication.

The analysis of convex vs. non-convex environments directly applies to my setting: my Heston market with transaction costs may have non-convexities (e.g., due to partial observability of variance, non-convex transaction costs). The finding that DH fails in non-convex environments with multimodal Q* suggests that my JEPA representation, which learns a structured representation of price history, may help by providing a better state representation that makes the problem more tractable. The sample efficiency results are directly relevant to my experiments where data may be limited. The game-theoretic interpretation of replication is also relevant for framing my problem.

Key Proofs: Theorem 1: Under concave increasing utility and convex cost function, optimal action-value function Q* is concave in action argument (unimodal). Theorem 2: (1) If Q*(s,a) is unimodal for all s, then π ↦ J_μ^π is unimodal on Π^c; (2) If there exists s such that Q*(s,a) is multimodal, then there exists initial distribution μ' such that π ↦ J_μ'^π is multimodal. Paper title: Deep Hedging with Reinforcement Learning: A Practical Framework for Option Risk Management
Overview: This paper presents a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for dynamic hedging of equity index option exposures under realistic transaction costs and position limits. The authors hedge a normalized option-implied equity exposure by trading the underlying index ETF, using the option surface and macro variables only as state information. Building on the deep hedging paradigm of Buehler et al., they design a leak-free environment, a cost-aware reward function, and a lightweight stochastic actor-critic agent trained on daily end-of-day data panel constructed from SPX/SPY implied volatility term structure, skew, realized volatility, and macro rate context. On a fixed train/validation/test split, the learned policy improves risk-adjusted performance versus no-hedge, momentum, and volatility-targeting baselines.
Technology stack: Two-layer MLP (256 hidden units, tanh activations), squashed Gaussian policy, actor-critic with GAE, entropy regularization (β=0.01), Adam optimizer, gradient clipping at 1.0, cosine learning rate schedule. Python, PyTorch (implied). Code available at https://github.com/tlucius16/deep-hedging-rl.
Improvements: Practical implementation with leak-free environment and deterministic pipeline. Cost-aware reward function with basis point scaling. Comprehensive evaluation including blended overlays, regime attribution, and statistical significance testing. Interpretable features enabling auditability.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Practical implementation of deep hedging for SPX/SPY exposures with realistic execution constraints; (2) Leak-free environment design with deterministic pipeline; (3) Cost-aware reward function with basis point scaling; (4) Lightweight actor-critic agent with interpretable features; (5) Comprehensive evaluation including blended overlays, regime attribution, and statistical significance testing.
Methodology: Hedging environment: observation matrix W×F (window × features), actions a_t ∈ [-a_max, a_max] (hedge levels), transaction costs c_t = κ|a_t - a_{t-1}|, per-step PnL p_t = a_t R_{t+1} - c_t, reward r_t = 10⁴ p_t. Features: ATM IV (30d, 91d), term structure slope, 25-delta put/call skew, VIX, 10Y yield, realized/historical vols (21d, 30d, 91d). RL framework: two-layer MLP (256 hidden, tanh) outputs mean μ_θ(s_t), log std, state value. Actions sampled from Normal, squashed with tanh, rescaled to [-a_max, a_max]. Entropy-regularized policy gradient with GAE. γ=0.99, gradient clipping at 1.0, cosine learning rate schedule, entropy coefficient 0.01.
Limitations on the work: Daily bars ignore intraday inventory management and execution costs. Generalization relies on walk-forward discipline. No option Greeks fed directly into state. Reward emphasizes mean/variance tradeoffs—more risk-sensitive objectives (drawdown, CVaR) can be slotted in. Statistically, results are suggestive rather than definitive—only GAE overlay has test Sharpe CI above zero, but overlaps with long SPY. Interpretability analysis is lightweight.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: SPX/SPY daily panel from 2005 onward. 18,018 trading days. IV fields populated on 96% of rows. Train: ≤2017-12-31, Validation: 2018-2019, Test: ≥2020-01-01. Features: ATM IV (30d, 91d), term structure slope (iv_91d - iv_30d), 25-delta put/call skew, VIX, 10Y yield, realized/historical vols (rv_21d, hvol_30d, hvol_91d).
