Paper title: Deep Hedging Under Realistic Market Frictions: A Regime-Conditional Empirical Study of Dynamic Option Hedging on Bitcoin Options
Overview: This paper tests whether deep hedging outperforms classical hedging methods under realistic transaction costs using five years of historical BTC options data from Deribit (2020-2024). The author compares three classical benchmarks (Black-Scholes delta, Leland's cost-adjusted volatility hedge, and Whalley-Wilmott no-trade band) against three deep hedging configurations (LSTM and feedforward network each trained with CVaR loss under two turnover-penalty weights), all under identical 5 basis point transaction cost assumption. On 11,546 out-of-sample test episodes, the Whalley-Wilmott strategy achieves statistically significant reduction in transaction costs relative to continuously-rebalanced strategies. All three deep hedging configurations underperform every classical benchmark on every metric measured, converging to a mean trade frequency statistically indistinguishable from continuous delta-hedging despite penalty weights spanning a twenty-fold range.
Technology stack: LSTM: 32 hidden units, single layer, processes full episode sequence. Feedforward: two hidden layers of 32 units, ReLU activations, applied independently at each timestep to 4-step lookback window. Output: scalar hedge position through 1.5·tanh(·), bounded to [-1.5, 1.5]. Named algorithms: LSTM, feedforward network, Adam optimizer, CVaR. No code availability stated.
Improvements: Fair, real-data comparison against classical cost-aware benchmarks. Demonstrates deep hedging underperformance on BTC options. Mechanistic explanation: absence of structural inductive bias toward sparsity. Regime-conditional analysis. Block bootstrap for statistical significance.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Fair, real-data test of deep hedging against classical cost-aware benchmarks (not just frictionless delta hedging); (2) Demonstrates that deep hedging underperforms Whalley-Wilmott no-trade band on real BTC options data; (3) Shows that turnover penalty across a twenty-fold range and two architectures does not induce sparse trading; (4) Provides mechanistic explanation: absence of structural inductive bias toward sparsity; (5) Regime-conditional analysis showing P&L advantage is regime-dependent while cost advantage persists.
Methodology: Problem: hedge short BTC option, rebalance hourly using BTC. P&L: P&L_opt,t = -(V_t - V_{t-1}), P&L_hedge,t = δ_{t-1}(S_t - S_{t-1}), C_t = |δ_t - δ_{t-1}|S_t(k/2). Terminal hedging error Π = Σ(P&L_opt,t + P&L_hedge,t - C_t). Classical benchmarks: BS delta (Equation 1), Leland (Equation 3), Whalley-Wilmott (Equation 4, λ=60). Deep hedging: state = (moneyness, TTM, IV, BS delta, call/put indicator), LSTM and feedforward architectures, CVaR loss (Equation 9) with turnover penalty. Training: padded episodes (24 steps), Adam optimizer, early stopping. Evaluation: block bootstrap (5,000 resamples, blocking by sampled day).
Limitations on the work: Single continuous out-of-sample test window (Sep 2023-Dec 2024) including large BTC rally. Limited training data (8,922 episodes, 24 timesteps each). Historical data coverage limited to 61 monthly snapshots (first of month). Fixed 5 bps transaction cost assumption. Whalley-Wilmott λ=60 calibrated by inspection. Deep hedging architecture scope limited to three configurations. Single asset class (BTC options). No code availability stated.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Deribit BTC options, 61 monthly snapshots (first of each month) from January 2020 to December 2024. Downsampled to hourly snapshots. Final cleaned dataset: 490,229 rows. Train: Dec 2019-Dec 2022 (187,961 rows), Validation: Jan-Aug 2023 (64,474 rows), Test: Sep 2023-Dec 2024 (237,894 rows). Transaction cost: k=5 bps round-trip (2.5 bps per trade).
Evaluation Metric Used: Mean terminal P&L, standard deviation, CVaR (95%), mean transaction cost, mean turnover, mean number of trades per episode, maximum drawdown.

Usage/ Benefits: Provides fair, real-data comparison of deep hedging vs. classical cost-aware benchmarks. Offers Whalley-Wilmott benchmark with λ=60 calibration. Paper title: Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithms for Option Hedging
Overview: This paper compares the performance of eight DRL algorithms in the context of dynamic hedging: Monte Carlo Policy Gradient (MCPG), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), four variants of Deep Q-Learning (DQL), and two variants of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG). Two of these variants (Dueling DQL and Dueling Double DQL) represent novel applications to dynamic hedging. The authors use Black-Scholes delta hedge as baseline and simulate data using a GJR-GARCH(1,1) model. Results show MCPG, followed by PPO, obtain the best performance in terms of root semi-quadratic penalty (RSQP). MCPG is the only algorithm to outperform the Black-Scholes delta hedge baseline with the allotted computational budget.
Technology stack: Feedforward neural networks for policy and value functions. Hyperparameters selected via grid search: learning rates in [0.001, 0.0001, 0.00001], batch sizes in [64, 128, 256], hidden layers in [2, 3, 4], hidden sizes in [64, 128, 256]. 81 combinations tested. All datasets and code publicly available.
Improvements: First systematic comparison of eight DRL algorithms for dynamic hedging. First application of Dueling DQL and Dueling Double DQL to dynamic hedging. Demonstrates MCPG outperforms all other algorithms including TD3, DDPG, and DQL variants.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Standard comparison of performance and time efficiency of most widely used DRL algorithms for dynamic hedging optimization; (2) Evaluation of variants not previously explored in DRL dynamic hedging literature: Dueling DQL and Dueling Double DQL; (3) Demonstration that Monte Carlo algorithms (MCPG, PPO) outperform Temporal-Difference algorithms (DQL, DDPG) in sparse reward environments.
Methodology: Dynamic hedging as MDP: state = (t/T_c, S_t/S_0, V_t/V_0), action = X_{t+1} (number of shares), reward = -R²·1_{R>0} at terminal step. Policy gradient approach (actor-only) for MCPG. Actor-critic for DDPG, TD3, PPO. Value-based for DQL variants. GJR-GARCH(1,1) model for log-returns: Y_t = μ + ε_t, ε_t = σ_t·e_t, σ_t² = ν_0 + (ν + λI_{t-1})ε_{t-1}² + ξσ_{t-1}². Training: 500,000 updates with early stopping.
Limitations on the work: Only one option type (call) and one market model (GJR-GARCH) tested. Limited computational budget affects TD algorithms. No transaction costs explicitly considered. No comparison with deep hedging (supervised learning) approaches. Hyperparameter tuning limited to 81 combinations. The study does not test higher-dimensional problems.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated price paths from GJR-GARCH(1,1) model calibrated to monthly S&P 500 prices from 2000/11/15 to 2024/10/15. Parameters: μ=0.00533410, ν_0=0.00018216, ν=0.00026564, ξ=0.70611408, λ=0.34275732. Training: 2^19 paths, validation: 2^17 paths, test: 10 sets of 2^17 paths each.
Evaluation Metric Used: Root Semi-Quadratic Penalty (RSQP): ρ^RSQP(R) = √(E[R²·1_{R>0}])
keywords: Deep reinforcement learning, option hedging, DQL, DDPG, TD3, PPO, MCPG, GJR-GARCH, RSQP.

The RSQP risk measure is an alternative to CVaR that I could consider. The GJR-GARCH model is similar to my Heston setup in capturing stochastic volatility. I can use the RSQP metric, the algorithm comparison results, and the network architectures as baselines. The finding that MCPG is robust to hyperparameters is useful for my implementation.

Paper title: Direct Reinforcement for Derivatives: Enhancing Intraday Deep Hedging via Risk-Averse Reward Shaping
Overview: This paper proposes a Deep Hedging framework with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for autonomous intraday derivatives trading. The authors construct a finite-horizon MDP where an agent manages straddle multi-leg inventories to neutralize non-linear Gamma risk. The system uses a 55-dimensional state space with temporal positional-context encoding and a custom reward function that heavily penalizes drawdown. Experimental validation on out-of-sample NIFTY50 episodes from January-December 2025 yielded a total PnL of Rs. 72,60,507.95, win rate of 65.73%, and Sharpe ratio of 8.23.
Technology stack: PPO with actor-critic. MLP with Tanh activation. Architecture: 64x64. MultiDiscrete([3,3]) action space. Named algorithms: PPO, PPO-Clip.
Improvements: First application of DRL to intraday multi-leg options trading. Custom reward function with drawdown penalty. 55-dimensional state space with cyclical time encoding. Demonstrates Theta-Gamma trade-off management.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) First application of DRL to intraday options trading with multi-leg instruments (straddle); (2) Custom reward function with drawdown penalty for professional risk management; (3) 55-dimensional state space with cyclical time encoding for positional context; (4) Demonstrates model-free RL can internalize Theta-Gamma trade-off in high-frequency settings.
Methodology: MDP formulation: state = 55 features (market dynamics, technical signals, time encodings), action = MultiDiscrete([3,3]) for Call/Put legs (Hold/Add/Offload), reward = PnL_t/max(P_deployed,1) - λ·max(0,Drawdown_t)/max(P_deployed,1). PPO-Clip objective: L^CLIP(θ) = Ê_t[min(r_t(θ)Â_t, clip(r_t(θ), 1-ε, 1+ε)Â_t)]. Black-Scholes-Merton for option pricing. Atomic enforcement prevents naked positions. Auto-square off at 3:15 PM.
Limitations on the work: Execution frictions: atomic execution ignores lagging risk (legs filled at different times). Pricing assumptions: dynamic implied volatility from lagged India VIX with fallback chain; no stochastic volatility or smile dynamics. Stationarity: training data (2021-2023) captures particular market regimes. No Level-2 order book data. Single market (NIFTY50).

Paper title: Fast Deep Hedging with Second-Order Optimization
Overview: This paper proposes a second-order optimization scheme for deep hedging. The authors leverage pathwise differentiability to construct a curvature matrix, approximated as block-diagonal and Kronecker-factored to efficiently precondition gradients. They evaluate on hedging a cliquet option on a stock with stochastic volatility by trading in the spot and vanilla options. The second-order scheme can optimize the policy in 1/4 of the number of steps that standard adaptive moment-based optimization (Adam) takes.
Technology stack: RNN with LSTM cells (32 hidden units), residual blocks, RMSNorm, He initialization. DH-KFAC algorithm with trust-region size decay. Adam optimizer for comparison. Python, Tensorflow (implied). No code availability stated.
Improvements: First application of second-order optimization to deep hedging. New damping scheme for KFAC. Floating grid formulation for option hedging. 4x speedup over Adam.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Second-order optimization scheme for deep hedging using Kronecker-factored curvature matrix; (2) New damping scheme based on optimal scale; (3) Floating grid formulation for option hedging; (4) Demonstration of 4x speedup over Adam on cliquet hedging.
Methodology: Second-order optimization: precondition gradients with inverse of Kronecker-factored curvature matrix. DH-KFAC algorithm: computes pseudo-gradient, updates A and G matrices, computes eigenvectors, preconditions gradient, applies trust-region step size selection. Floating grid: at each time step, trade options with same moneyness and time to maturity; portfolio represented approximately via recurrent connections. Cliquet option: ψ(x) = max[Σ min(x_t/x_{t-1} - 1, μ), 0]. Heston model for stochastic volatility.
Limitations on the work: Implementation not optimized for wall-clock time (though speedup exists). Tested only on cliquet option with Heston model. Floating grid formulation requires approximate portfolio representation. No comparison with other second-order methods. Computational overhead may be smaller for larger networks.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated Heston paths: x_0=1, κ=8, v_0=θ=0.0625, ξ=1.0, ρ=-0.7. 700,000 paths for T=240 steps. 19 vanilla options at each step. Cliquet: maturity T, cap μ=0.015, reset dates τ_1=20, τ_2=40, ..., τ_12=T. Transaction costs: c^(1)=1e-4, c^(i)=1e-2 for i>1. Risk aversion γ=1000.
Evaluation Metric Used: Validation loss, gradient variance, largest eigenvalue of preconditioner, PnL distribution, standard deviation, skewness.
keywords: Deep Hedging, Cliquet, Second-Order Optimization, FKAC, Natural Gradient Descent.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides second-order optimization scheme for deep hedging. New damping scheme. Floating grid formulation. 4x speedup over Adam. Analysis of learned hedging policy.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it addresses the training efficiency of deep hedging models, which is a practical concern for my experiments. The second-order optimization scheme could potentially accelerate training of my JEPA-based hedging policy. The floating grid formulation is specific to option hedging but demonstrates the importance of architecture design. The curvature matrix approach is mathematically sophisticated but may be overkill for my smaller networks. I can use the DH-KFAC algorithm as an alternative optimizer and the evaluation methodology (validation loss curves, PnL distributions) for my experiments. The finding that option hedging reduces PnL std by 50% is relevant to my use of options as hedging instruments.
Challenges: Implementation not optimized for wall-clock time. Tested only on cliquet option. Floating grid requires approximate portfolio representation. Computational overhead may vary with network size.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses KFAC, EKFAC, RNN-KFAC from prior work.

Paper title: Hedging Targeted Risks with Reinforcement Learning: Application to Life Insurance Contracts with Embedded Guarantees
Overview: This paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed to optimize the hedging of specific, user-defined risk factors—referred to as targeted risks—in financial instruments affected by multiple sources of uncertainty. The methodology uses Shapley value decompositions to establish source of risk grouping's contribution to projected contract cash flows, providing clear attribution of P&L to distinct risk categories. Leveraging this decomposition, the authors apply deep RL to hedge only the targeted risks, while leaving non-targeted risks mostly unaffected. They introduce a joint neural network architecture in which the agent network utilizes risk estimates from a risk measurement neural network to stabilize the hedging strategy. Numerical experiments show the approach outperforms delta hedging and traditional deep hedging for variable annuities.
Technology stack: Hedging network: 4 hidden layers, 56 neurons each, ReLU activation, ReLU-negative output activation. CVaR network: 3 hidden layers, 56 neurons each, ReLU activation, identity output. Glorot and Bengio initialization. Adam optimizer. Python, TensorFlow. Dropout p=0.5. Code available at GitHub.
Improvements: First deep RL framework for hedging targeted risks using Shapley decompositions. Joint architecture with risk measurement network. Application to variable annuities with embedded guarantees. Demonstrates superiority over delta hedging and traditional deep hedging.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Deep RL framework for hedging targeted risks using Shapley decompositions; (2) Novel application to variable annuities with embedded guarantees; (3) Joint neural network architecture with risk measurement network for local risk penalization; (4) Demonstration that targeted hedging outperforms traditional delta hedging and deep hedging; (5) Extension of Shapley decomposition to cover entire hedging period rather than single time points.
Methodology: Shapley decomposition: P&L decomposed into contributions from different risk groups: P&L_T = Σ_k C^(k) + Θ_T. Targeted hedging optimization: minimize L(θ) = ||1_{H_s^(T) + C^(T) < 0}(H_s^(T) + C^(T))||²_L2 + Σ_{k≠T} ||H_s^(k)||²_L2 + ||Θ_T^{V_θ}||²_L2. Local risk penalization: RC_α(θ) = Σ_{t=0}^{T-1} CVaR_α(-NGL_{t+1}^δ | F_t). Objective: O_α^p(θ) = L(θ) + p·RC_α(θ). Two FFNNs: hedging network and CVaR estimation network.
Limitations on the work: All experiments on simulated data. Only European-style variable annuities (GMMB, GMWB). No real market data. Computational cost of nested simulations. Ad hoc hyperparameter tuning (no formal procedure). FFNNs chosen for flexibility, not optimized for sequential structure. No code availability (available at GitHub).
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: GMMB and GMWB variable annuities with T=240 months. Two funds: Assumption mixed fund and RBC bond fund. Market dynamics: three-factor Gaussian model for interest rates, EGARCH for equity indices, mixed fund model. Hedging instruments: risk-free asset and equity futures on two indices. Training: 100,000 paths, 50 epochs (GMMB) or 100 epochs (GMWB), batch size 1000.
Evaluation Metric Used: Expected P&L, Variance, CVaR at 95%, Risk allocations for each source of risk group.
keywords: Deep hedging, reinforcement learning, risk allocation, Shapley decomposition, variable annuities.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides Shapley decomposition for risk attribution. Targeted hedging framework. Joint architecture with risk measurement network. Local risk penalization. Risk allocation evaluation metrics. Application to variable annuities.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it introduces a framework for hedging targeted risks using Shapley decompositions, which is conceptually related to my goal of using a JEPA-learned representation to inform hedging decisions. The idea of decomposing P&L into contributions from different risk sources is analogous to decomposing the state representation into meaningful components. The joint neural network architecture with a separate risk measurement network is similar to my planned use of JEPA as a representation network alongside the policy network. The local risk penalization (CVaR of one-period losses) is an alternative to my terminal CVaR objective. However, the application is to insurance contracts, not options. I can use the Shapley decomposition methodology, the joint architecture design, and the risk allocation evaluation metrics. The finding that targeted hedging outperforms traditional deep hedging is relevant to my hypothesis that a more structured representation (JEPA) will improve hedging.
Challenges: Computational cost of nested simulations. Ad hoc hyperparameter tuning. FFNNs not optimized for sequential structure. No real market data. Only European-style variable annuities.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses Shapley value decomposition from cooperative game theory.

Paper title: Towards a Fast and Robust Deep Hedging Approach
Overview: This paper presents a robust Deep Hedging framework for pricing and hedging option portfolios that significantly improves training efficiency and model robustness. The authors propose a neural model for training model embeddings which utilizes paths of several advanced equity option models with stochastic volatility to learn relationships between hedging strategies. A key advantage is the ability to rapidly and reliably adapt to new market regimes through recalibration of a low-dimensional embedding vector, rather than retraining the entire network. The framework works well with data generated by complex models and can serve as a construction basis for an efficient and robust simulation tool for systematic development of an entirely model-independent hedging strategy.
Technology stack: Neural network: 3 inner layers, 128 neurons each, SELU activation. Batch size 1024, Adam optimizer, 1000 epochs, exponentially decaying learning rate (initial 0.0005, final 0.0001). Python, TensorFlow. No code availability stated.
Improvements: First application of task embedding to deep hedging. Ability to adapt to new market regimes via low-dimensional embedding recalibration. Demonstrated robustness to model uncertainty. PNN outperforms single-task networks with limited data.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Task-embedded neural network (PNN) for deep hedging under model uncertainty; (2) Ability to adapt to new market regimes by recalibrating only low-dimensional embedding vector; (3) Demonstration that PNN outperforms single-task networks when training data is limited; (4) Analysis of PnL distributions on parameter space of models used to learn embeddings; (5) Framework works with complex models (Heston, Heston with jumps, BNS).
Methodology: Task-embedded neural network (PNN): embedding layer maps TaskID (model index) to parameter vector p_i ∈ R^l; concatenated with input features; main network shared across tasks. Training: each task (model) has n sample paths; embedding vectors fine-tuned during training. Recalibration: for new task, only new parameter vector p_new ∈ R^l is learned. Models: GBM, Heston, Heston with jumps, BNS. Option: short ATM European call with K=1, S_0=1, T=30/365. Daily rebalancing.
Limitations on the work: Tested only on simulated data (GBM, Heston, Heston with jumps, BNS). No real market data. No transaction costs in main experiments. Simplified setting for proof-of-concept. No detailed analysis of dependency of PnL on parameter space. Future work: evaluate on real financial data with market frictions.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: GBM (volatility uniformly distributed on [0.1, 0.8]), Heston, Heston with jumps, BNS. 50 different underlyings for stochastic volatility models. Option quotes for indices (DAX, STOXX50E, S&P 500, CAC) and single equity indices. 40,000 simulated paths per model for testing.
Evaluation Metric Used: PnL distribution, standard deviation of PnL, mean variance, median variance, maximum variance.
keywords: Deep Hedging, Parameterized Neural Networks, Multi-Task Learning, Quantitative Finance, Hedging Strategy.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides task-embedded neural network for deep hedging. Ability to adapt to new market regimes with limited data. Framework for hedging under model uncertainty. Embedding visualization (t-SNE). PnL distribution analysis.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it introduces task-embedded neural networks for deep hedging under model uncertainty, which is conceptually similar to my use of JEPA to learn a representation that generalizes across market conditions. The embedding layer that encodes different models/tasks is analogous to a learned representation that captures the essential features of the market. The finding that recalibrating only the low-dimensional embedding vector is sufficient to adapt to new market regimes is directly relevant to my goal of using JEPA to learn a robust representation that can be fine-tuned for different hedging scenarios. The PNN architecture provides a template for integrating a learned representation into a hedging policy. I can use the task embedding approach as a baseline for comparison with my JEPA representation. The finding that PNN outperforms single-task networks with limited data is relevant to my data efficiency goals.
Challenges: Tested only on simulated data. No real market data. No transaction costs in main experiments. Simplified setting for proof-of-concept. No detailed analysis of parameter dependence.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses multi-task learning and task embedding from prior work.

Paper title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Hedging
Overview: This paper introduces uncertainty quantification to the deep hedging framework by training a deep ensemble of five independent LSTM networks under Heston stochastic volatility with proportional transaction costs. The ensemble's disagreement at each time step provides a per-time-step confidence measure that is strongly predictive of hedging performance: the learned strategy outperforms Black-Scholes delta on approximately 80% of paths when model agreement is high, but on fewer than 20% when disagreement is elevated. The author proposes a CVaR-optimized blending strategy that combines the ensemble's hedge with the classical Black-Scholes delta, weighted by model uncertainty. The blend improves on Black-Scholes delta by 35-80 basis points in CVaR across several Heston calibrations, and on Whalley-Wilmott strategy by 100-250 basis points.
Technology stack: LSTM: 2 layers, 32 hidden units per layer, fully connected output layer. Deep ensemble: 5 independent networks. Blending: sigmoid parameterization. Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.01 for blending, 2000 iterations). pfhedge library, PyTorch. No code availability stated.
Improvements: First application of uncertainty quantification to deep hedging. Demonstration that ensemble disagreement is predictive of hedging performance. CVaR-optimized blending strategy. Analysis of uncertainty drivers. Regime-dependent inversion of uncertainty-performance relationship.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) First application of uncertainty quantification (deep ensembles) to deep hedging; (2) Demonstration that ensemble disagreement is predictive of hedging performance; (3) CVaR-optimized blending strategy combining ensemble and Black-Scholes delta; (4) Analysis of drivers of ensemble uncertainty (moneyness not volatility); (5) Regime-dependent inversion of uncertainty-performance relationship.
Methodology: Deep hedging with LSTM: state x_t = (log(S_t/K), τ_t, √v_t, δ_{t-1}), network outputs hedge ratio δ_t. Training objective: entropic risk measure ρ_a(P&L) = (1/a)log E[exp(-a·P&L)], a=1. Deep ensemble: 5 independently trained networks; uncertainty ψ_t = standard deviation of ensemble outputs. Blending: δ_t^blend = (1-α_t)δ̄_t + α_t δ_t^BS, α_t = sigmoid(β_0 + β_1 ψ_t). Optimize β_0, β_1 to minimize CVaR or entropic risk. Heston model: dS_t = S_t√v_t dW_t^S, dv_t = κ(θ-v_t)dt + σ√v_t dW_t^v.
Limitations on the work: All experiments on simulated data (Heston model). Only European call options on single underlying. Uncertainty quantification relies exclusively on deep ensembles. Blending uses BS delta with fixed volatility. Architecture and hyperparameters not subjected to systematic ablation. No real market data. No transaction cost savings from options.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated Heston paths: baseline (σ=0.4, ρ=-0.7), high vol-of-vol (σ=0.8, ρ=-0.7), low correlation (σ=0.4, ρ=-0.3). κ=2, θ=0.04, v_0=0.04, c=5e-4. T=0.5 years, n=126 time steps. 10,000 test paths. 7,000 training paths for blending.
Evaluation Metric Used: Mean P&L, Standard deviation of P&L, CVaR at 5%, Win rate, Uncertainty (ensemble disagreement).
keywords: Deep hedging, uncertainty quantification, deep ensembles, stochastic volatility, transaction costs, risk management.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides deep ensemble for uncertainty quantification in deep hedging. CVaR-optimized blending strategy. Analysis of uncertainty drivers. Evaluation methodology (paired bootstrap). Performance across Heston calibrations.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it introduces uncertainty quantification to deep hedging, which is directly related to my use of JEPA to learn a representation that captures uncertainty in price history. The deep ensemble approach provides a method for measuring confidence in the learned policy, which could complement my JEPA representation. The finding that ensemble uncertainty is predictive of hedging performance (80% win rate when confident) supports my hypothesis that a good representation should know when it's uncertain. The CVaR-optimized blending strategy is a practical approach to combining a learned policy with a classical hedge, which I could use with my JEPA-based policy. The finding that the ensemble's advantage comes from transaction cost savings (trading 4x less) is relevant to my transaction cost setting. The analysis of drivers of uncertainty (moneyness not volatility) is interesting for understanding what my JEPA representation might capture. I can use the deep ensemble methodology as an alternative to JEPA for uncertainty quantification, and the blending strategy as a baseline.
Challenges: Simulated data only. European call options only. Deep ensembles computationally expensive. Blending uses BS delta with fixed volatility. Architecture not systematically ablated. No real market data.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses paired bootstrap for statistical significance.

Paper title: Hedging of Financial Derivative Contracts via Monte Carlo Tree Search
Overview: This paper interprets the construction of replication strategies for pricing and hedging of derivative contracts in incomplete markets as a "game with the world", where one player (the investor) bets on what will happen and the other player (the market) decides what will happen. Inspired by the success of Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) in games and stochastic multiperiod planning problems, the author introduces this algorithm as a method for replication in the presence of risk and market friction. Unlike model-free reinforcement learning methods (such as Q-learning), MCTS makes explicit use of an environment model (market simulator), which allows it to plan for consequences of decisions prior to execution. Experiments with AlphaZero variant on toy examples show MCTS is capable of maximizing utility of terminal wealth in settings where no external pricing information is available and rewards are granted only as result of contractual cashflows. MCTS has superior performance compared with DQN and comparable performance to deep hedging methods.
Technology stack: AlphaZero: MCTS with NNs. FF-NN: 59 shallow NNs (3 layers, 32 neurons each). DQN: Rainbow DQN. NN: 4 hidden layers, 256 neurons, batch normalization, ReLU, tanh for value, softmax for policy. Named algorithms: MCTS, UCT, AlphaZero, DQN, FF-NN. Code available on GitHub.
Improvements: First application of MCTS to derivatives hedging. Demonstration that MCTS can hedge without external pricing information. Comparison with DQN and deep hedging. Effectiveness across multiple market models and reward structures.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) First application of MCTS to derivatives hedging; (2) Interpretation of hedging as "game with the world"; (3) Demonstration that MCTS can hedge without external pricing information or intermediate rewards; (4) Comparison with DQN and deep hedging (FF-NN); (5) Demonstration of MCTS effectiveness across multiple market models (trinomial, GBM, Heston) and reward structures.
Methodology: Hedging as MDP: state s_t = (n_t, B_t, S_t, T-t), action = number of shares to hold, reward = utility of terminal wealth. MCTS: builds decision tree, uses UCB1 for tree policy, simulations for leaf evaluation. AlphaZero: MCTS with NNs for tree policy and value function, trained via imitation learning (expert = MCTS, apprentice = NN). Training: 1000 episodes per neural UCT iteration, 25 simulations per episode. NN training: 10 epochs, batch size 32. NN validation: rewards measured on 100 random paths.
Limitations on the work: Tested only on toy examples of simple market models and derivatives. MCTS more complex and difficult to maintain. Results harder to interpret. Training and execution slower than supervised learning. Choice of reward function and model calibration took considerable effort. Naive discretization does not work for many practical problems. No real market data.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: Trinomial market model (S_0=100, volatility=30%), GBM (S_0=100, volatility=30%), Heston (S_0=100, α=1, b=0.04, ρ=-0.7, σ=2, V_0=0.04). Derivative: short European call (K=100, T=60), call spreads (K1=100, K2=110 or 120). Transaction costs: proportional, η=0.01. Daily rebalancing.
Evaluation Metric Used: Test reward, Portfolio gains, Accumulated transaction costs, Average quadratic loss, Normalized loss.
keywords: Reinforcement learning, Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), pricing and hedging of derivative contracts, AlphaZero, utility optimization.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides MCTS as alternative to deep hedging. Game-theoretic interpretation of hedging. AlphaZero architecture for hedging. Demonstration of effectiveness in sparse reward settings. Comparison with DQN and FF-NN. Handling of varying reward structures.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it introduces MCTS as an alternative to deep hedging for derivative replication, which provides a different perspective on the hedging problem. The "game with the world" interpretation is conceptually interesting and aligns with the adversarial nature of financial markets. The finding that MCTS outperforms DQN in sparse reward settings is relevant to my use of terminal CVaR objectives. The AlphaZero architecture, which combines MCTS with neural networks, is similar to my planned use of JEPA as a representation network alongside a policy network. However, MCTS is computationally expensive and may not scale to my Heston simulation with partial observability. I can use MCTS as an alternative baseline and the game-theoretic interpretation for framing my problem. The paper also demonstrates that MCTS can handle transaction costs and varying utility functions.
Challenges: MCTS more complex and slower than supervised learning. Results harder to interpret. Choice of reward function and model calibration effort. Naive discretization issues. Tested only on toy examples.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses UCT convergence guarantees from Kocsis and Szepesvári (2006).

Paper title: Market-Making and Hedging with Market Impact using Deep Reinforcement Learning
Overview: This paper uses a deep reinforcement learning framework with deep neural networks to approximate the optimal quoting and hedging strategies of a market maker taking into consideration market friction. The framework can consider a wide range of inventory management and PnL distribution preferences that would be infeasible with analytical methods. The authors show that networks can learn theoretical optimal strategies well, and demonstrate observations when applied to generalized settings. Prior knowledge of desired market-making behavior can be incorporated using a partially monotonic network, which increases reliability.
Technology stack: Feedforward neural networks: 15 nodes, 4 layers, Leaky ReLU activation, tanh for bid/ask spreads, linear for hedge rate. Partially monotonic network: constrained (non-negative weights) and unconstrained blocks. Named algorithms: Deep RL, policy gradient, Adam, partially monotonic networks.
Improvements: First DRL framework for market-making with hedging and market impact. Can optimize generalized objectives (CVaR) infeasible for analytical methods. Model-free approach. Partially monotonic network for prior knowledge incorporation.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) DRL framework for market-making with hedging and market impact; (2) Can optimize generalized objectives (CVaR) that are infeasible for analytical methods; (3) Model-free approach requiring no specific model; (4) Partially monotonic neural network for incorporating prior knowledge; (5) Demonstration that neural networks learn PDE-optimal strategies.
Methodology: Market-making with RL: state = (t_k, q_t, z_t^b, z_t^a), action = (δ^b, δ^a, w), reward = objective function (mean-variance or CVaR). Market model: dS_t = σdW_t + kw_t dt (linear permanent impact). Order flow: Poisson processes with logistic intensity functions. Neural networks: NN_b, NN_a, NN_w for bid, ask, hedge rate. Training: 10^6 paths, batch size 4096, 20 epochs. PDE baseline: explicit Euler scheme on 2000*200 grid.
Limitations on the work: Tested only on simulated USD/CNH market data. Single asset. No real market data. Partially monotonic network restricts expressiveness. Computational cost of PDE baseline limits comparison. Market impact model simplified (linear permanent impact).
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: USD/CNH market. S_0=70000 pips, σ=50 pips·day^{-1/2}, k=0.005 pips·MS^{-1}. Hedging cost: φ=0.1 pips, η=0.00001 pips·MS^{-1}·day. Order sizes: 1, 5, 10, 20 MS with probabilities 0.76, 0.15, 0.075, 0.015. Inventory limit: Q=100 MS. T=0.05 day, n=100 steps. γ=0.0005 pips^{-1}MS^{-1}.
Evaluation Metric Used: Objective value, PnL, PnL distribution, Bid/ask quotes, Hedging rate, Inventory.
keywords: FX, Market-making, Machine learning, Reinforcement learning, Neural network, Market impact.
Usage/ Benefits: Provides DRL framework for market-making with hedging. CVaR optimization. Partially monotonic network for prior knowledge. Model-free approach. Comparison with PDE solution.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is tangentially relevant because it addresses market-making and hedging with market impact, which is a different problem from my single-option hedging but shares the RL framework. The partially monotonic neural network is interesting for incorporating prior knowledge into the policy, which could be relevant if I want to enforce monotonicity in my JEPA representation. The CVaR optimization in a market-making context is related to my CVaR objective. However, the paper does not use learned representations—it uses hand-crafted features. The application is to FX market-making, not option hedging on simulated Heston. I can use the CVaR optimization methodology and the partially monotonic network as references. The finding that neural networks can replicate PDE-optimal strategies is a good validation of RL for financial control problems.
Challenges: Tested only on simulated data. Single asset. Partially monotonic network restricts expressiveness. Computational cost of PDE baseline. Simplified market impact model.
Key Proofs: None stated. References PDE solution from prior work.

Paper title: Climate-Dyna Deep Hedging for XVAs: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning, Residual Climate HVA, and Hedge-Instrument Discovery
Overview: This paper formulates deep hedging for XVAs as a residual control problem where the inherited XVA hedge is credited first, and model-based RL trades only an incremental climate overlay against the remaining liability. The framework combines a finite-horizon Riccati controller as an analytical prior with paired structural-residual world-model Dyna planning, risk-sensitive policy learning, and independent deployment certification. Experiments in a public-data-calibrated semi-synthetic EU ETS environment show that crediting the inherited hedge lowers the mean climate charge from 1.517 to 0.906, and the learned overlay lowers it to 0.831 against a 0.821 exact floor.
Technology stack: Not specified in detail. Likely PyTorch or TensorFlow. OSQP for QP solving. ABIDES/MockLOB for execution. No code availability stated.
Improvements: First framework for residual climate HVA using deep RL. Combines Riccati analytical prior with Dyna model-based RL. Introduces independent deployment certification. Provides formal guarantees for safety, DRO, and CVaR estimation.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Unified residual climate-XVA framework connecting clean value, certainty-equivalent desk XVA, inherited hedge, optimal climate overlays, residual climate HVA, and instrument value; (2) Exact finite-horizon Riccati overlay used as benchmark and analytical prior for nonlinear deep hedging; (3) Climate-Dyna method combining constrained structural-residual world modeling, importance-corrected planning, risk-sensitive policy learning, ensemble robustness, and independent deployment certification.
Methodology: Residual control formulation: inherited hedge credited first, overlay optimized against residual liability Ĉ_clim = C_clim - (I⁰)ᵀΔH⁰,inc + ΔΓ⁰. Riccati anchor: exact finite-horizon solution for linear-Gaussian case. Climate-Dyna: paired world model with structural-residual decomposition, prioritized Dyna rollouts, risk-sensitive residual policy, ensemble robustness, independent gate for deployment. CVaR optimization via Rockafellar-Uryasev program with temperature-tilted quantile sampling.
Limitations on the work: Synthetic market only (SSVI→Dupire→VIX with ABIDES/MockLOB execution). Simplified execution and microstructure. Approximation in safety-layer modeling (linearized CBF surrogates). Estimator variance and controller tuning. Trust-region and robustness assumptions. Metric coverage (CVaR at given α). Generalization across books and instruments. Governance and compliance boundaries. Computational constraints.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Semi-synthetic EU ETS data calibrated to public data from 2012-2025. EEX auctions for allowance prices, EXH9 utilities ETF, ECB rates, CISS bond component, EU Transaction Log emissions, EBA PD/LGD ranges. Chronological split: 2012-2018 training, 2019-2020 validation, 2021-2025 out-of-distribution testing.
Evaluation Metric Used: Mean exact target-policy regret, gated deployment acceptance rate, material harm rate, CVaR, mean P&L.
keywords: Climate risk, XVA, Deep hedging, Model-based Reinforcement learning, Risk-sensitive control.
Usage/ Benefits: Residual control formulation for hedging inherited positions. Riccati anchor for stable learning. Paired world model for counterfactual analysis. CVaR concentration results. Telemetry-to-governance mapping for explainability. Independent deployment certification.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it introduces a framework for residual control where an analytical prior (Riccati) is combined with model-based RL, which is conceptually similar to my use of JEPA as a learned representation to improve hedging. The paired climate-on/climate-off worlds methodology for isolating incremental effects is analogous to my comparison between JEPA-based and baseline representations. The risk-sensitive CVaR objective and the use of independent certification for deployment align with my need for robust evaluation. However, the application is to climate XVA, not option hedging on simulated Heston, and the state includes climate-specific variables. I can use the residual control formulation, the Riccati anchor as a baseline, the CVaR concentration results, and the telemetry-to-governance mapping for my experiments. The safety filter architecture (CBF-QP) is a potential addition to my hedging policy.
Challenges: Synthetic market only. Simplified execution. Linearized CBF surrogates. Estimator variance. Trust-region assumptions. Metric coverage. Generalization across books and instruments. Computational constraints.
Key Proofs: Theorem 1 (robust forward invariance of safety set), Proposition 1 (minimal-deviation projection), Theorem 2 (KL-DRO upper bound), Theorem 3 (concentration of temperature-tilted CVaR estimator), Theorem 4 (CVaR trust-region improvement), Theorem 5 (feasibility persistence under tail guards), Proposition 2 (negative-advantage suppression by sign-consistency gate). Proofs in Appendix A.

Paper title: Robust Risk-Aware Option Hedging
Overview: This paper showcases the potential of robust risk-aware reinforcement learning (RL) in mitigating risks associated with path-dependent financial derivatives. The authors leverage a policy gradient approach that optimizes robust risk-aware performance criteria, specifically applying it to hedging barrier options. They highlight how optimal hedging strategy undergoes distortions as agent moves from risk-averse to risk-seeking, and how the agent robustifies its strategy. They further investigate performance when data generating process varies from training DGP and demonstrate that robust strategies outperform non-robust ones.
Technology stack: Feedforward neural network (5 hidden layers, 35 neurons, SiLU). Distortion network (1 hidden layer, 10 neurons, SiLU). Named algorithms: RDEU, α-β risk measures, Wasserstein DRO, policy gradient.
Improvements: First application of robust risk-aware RL to barrier option hedging. Uses RDEU to model both risk-averse and gain-seeking behavior. Wasserstein ambiguity set for model uncertainty. Demonstrates phase transition in hedging behavior.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Apply robust risk-aware RL to option hedging using rank-dependent expected utility (RDEU); (2) Demonstrate how optimal hedging strategy changes as agent moves from risk-averse to risk-seeking; (3) Show robust strategies outperform non-robust ones under model misspecification; (4) Use Wasserstein ambiguity set to protect against model uncertainty; (5) Apply to barrier options (knock-in, knock-out).
Methodology: RDEU risk measure: R_g^U[Z] = -∫₀¹ U(F_Z^{-1}(s))γ(s)ds. α-β risk measure: special case of RDEU with distortion γ_p^{α,β}(u) = (1/η)[p·1(u≤α) + (1-p)·1(u≥β)]. Robust formulation: inf_φ sup_{θ∈Θ_φ} R_g^U[X^θ] where Θ_φ = {θ: d_p[X^θ, X^φ] ≤ ε}. Policy gradient via Theorem 5.1. Hedging features: t, S_t, M_t = min_{u≤t}S_u, 1[M_t>B], and Δ_{t-1} when transaction costs.
Limitations on the work: RDEU is not time-consistent (pre-commit strategies). Only barrier options tested. Single underlying. No real market data. Computational cost of robust optimization. Kernel density estimation for gradients may be inaccurate.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: Heston model with S₀=10, ν₀=0.3², μ=0.08, κ=3, θ=0.3², η=2, ρ=-0.5. Barrier options: T=1, B=8.5, K=10. 200 time steps, trading every 4 steps (50 trading dates). Model misspecification: κ=1, ρ=-0.1.
Evaluation Metric Used: P&L distribution, CVaR, expected utility, Wasserstein distance.
keywords: Reinforcement learning; option hedging; robustification; risk measures.
Usage/ Benefits: RDEU framework for risk-averse and gain-seeking behavior. Wasserstein DRO for model uncertainty. Gradient formulas for RDEU. Phase transition analysis. Evaluation methodology for robust strategies.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it introduces robust risk-aware RL using RDEU and Wasserstein ambiguity sets, which is directly applicable to my need for robustness in hedging under model uncertainty (partial observability of variance in Heston). The RDEU framework allows for both risk-averse and risk-seeking behavior, which could be useful for my CVaR objective. The phase transition finding is interesting for understanding how risk preferences affect hedging behavior. However, the paper does not use learned representations—it uses hand-crafted features. The application is to barrier options, not European calls. I can use the RDEU framework, the Wasserstein DRO formulation, the gradient formulas, and the evaluation methodology. The finding that robust strategies outperform non-robust ones under model misspecification supports my use of JEPA for robust representation learning.
Challenges: RDEU not time-consistent. Only barrier options tested. Single underlying. No real market data. Computational cost. Kernel density estimation.
Key Proofs: Theorem 5.1 (gradient formula for RDEU). Theorem 5.2 (inner gradient formula). Theorem 5.3 (outer gradient formula). No proofs in main text (references Jaimungal et al. 2022).

Paper title: Option Hedging with Risk Averse Reinforcement Learning
Overview: This paper shows how risk-averse reinforcement learning can be used to hedge options. The authors apply Trust Region Volatility Optimization (TRVO) to a vanilla option hedging environment, considering realistic factors such as discrete time and transaction costs. Realism makes the problem twofold: the agent must both minimize volatility and contain transaction costs, these tasks usually being in competition. They train a sheaf of agents each characterized by different risk aversion to span an efficient frontier on the volatility-p&l space. Results show the derived hedging strategy not only outperforms Black & Scholes delta hedge, but is also extremely robust and flexible, as it can efficiently hedge options with different characteristics and work on markets with different behaviors than what was used in training.
Technology stack: TRVO (Trust Region Volatility Optimization) algorithm. Policy network with 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons. Adam optimizer. No code availability stated.
Improvements: First application of TRVO to option hedging. Efficient frontier in volatility-P&L space. Demonstrates robustness to option characteristics and market behaviors.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Apply TRVO (risk-averse RL) to option hedging; (2) Create efficient frontier in volatility-P&L space by varying risk aversion; (3) Demonstrate robustness to different option characteristics and market behaviors; (4) Show RL agent outperforms delta hedge in both P&L and volatility; (5) Analyze how agent reduces hedging costs by delaying and reducing actions.
Methodology: MDP formulation: action a_t = h_t (hedge portfolio), state s_t = (S_t, C_t, ∂C/∂S_t, a_{t-1}), reward R(s_t,a_t) = f(ρ_t) where ρ_t = C_{t+k} - C_t - h_t(S_{t+k} - S_t) - c(n). TRVO objective: η_π = J_π + λν_π², where ν_π² is reward-volatility (minimizing variations between steps). Training: 10,000 scenarios, ~2,000 episodes, discount factor 0.999, max KL 0.001. Testing: 2,000 out-of-sample scenarios.
Limitations on the work: Only GBM with constant volatility tested (but tested on higher volatility scenarios). Zero financing cost. No real market data. Hedging portfolios with different maturities is difficult. The risk aversion parameter λ needs to be rescaled for different bid-ask levels.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: GBM with μ=0, σ=20%. 5 prices per day, 60-day maturity. Option price ~3.24, delta ~0.5. Transaction costs: tick size=0.05. Test scenarios: higher volatility (30%), different strikes (95, 105), portfolio of options (strikes 90-110).
Evaluation Metric Used: P&L, P&L volatility, reward volatility, transaction costs, efficient frontier.
keywords: Option Hedging, Reinforcement Learning, Transaction Costs.
Usage/ Benefits: TRVO algorithm for risk-averse option hedging. Efficient frontier analysis. Robustness to option characteristics and market behaviors. Evaluation metrics (P&L, volatility, costs).
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it demonstrates risk-averse RL for option hedging with transaction costs and shows the importance of the risk aversion parameter in shaping the hedging strategy. The TRVO algorithm with reward-volatility objective is an alternative to CVaR that I could consider. The efficient frontier analysis is directly applicable to my experiments with different risk aversion levels. The finding that the agent delays and reduces actions to control costs is relevant to my transaction cost setting. However, the paper does not use learned representations—it uses state (S_t, C_t, ∂C/∂S_t, a_{t-1}). The application is to vanilla options on GBM, not Heston. I can use the TRVO algorithm as an alternative to PPO, the efficient frontier methodology, and the evaluation metrics (P&L, volatility, costs). The finding that RL outperforms delta hedging supports my hypothesis.
Challenges: Only GBM with constant volatility. Zero financing cost. No real market data. Difficulty with portfolios of different maturities. λ rescaling for different bid-ask levels.
Key Proofs: None stated. References Bisi et al. (2019) for TRVO.

Paper title: VolGAN: A Generative Model for Arbitrage-Free Implied Volatility Surfaces
Overview: This paper introduces VolGAN, a generative model for arbitrage-free implied volatility surfaces. The model is trained on time series of implied volatility surfaces and underlying prices and is capable of generating realistic scenarios for joint dynamics of the implied volatility surface and the underlying asset. They illustrate performance by training on SPX implied volatility time series and show it learns covariance structure of co-movements in implied volatilities and generates realistic dynamics for VIX. The generative model simulates scenarios with non-Gaussian distributions of increments and time-varying correlations. Finally, they illustrate use of VolGAN to construct data-driven hedging strategies for option portfolios, showing these strategies can outperform Black-Scholes delta and delta-vega hedging.
Technology stack: VolGAN: Conditional GAN. Generator: 3-layer feedforward dense network (first two softplus, final affine), noise dimension 32, hidden sizes 16 and 32. Discriminator: 2-layer feedforward (softplus and sigmoid), hidden sizes 16 and 1. Smoothness penalty (Sobolev seminorm). LASSO regression. PCA. Code available at GitHub.
Improvements: First generative model for arbitrage-free IV surfaces. Uses smoothness penalty instead of BCE loss. Scenario re-weighting for arbitrage. Data-driven hedging via regression on generated scenarios. Automatic instrument selection.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Introduce VolGAN, a fully data-driven generative model for dynamic simulation of arbitrage-free implied volatility surfaces; (2) Train on SPX implied volatility time series, demonstrating ability to learn covariance structure and generate realistic VIX dynamics; (3) Show generative model can simulate non-Gaussian distributions and time-varying correlations; (4) Use VolGAN to compute data-driven hedging strategies that outperform Black-Scholes delta and delta-vega hedging; (5) Automatic selection of hedging instruments.
Methodology: VolGAN: conditional GAN with generator G(a_t,z_t) → (R̂_t, Δĝ_t(m,τ)), discriminator D(a_t,(R,Δg)). Smoothness penalty L_m and L_τ on generated surfaces. Scenario re-weighting: dP_β/dP_0 ∝ exp(-βΦ(σ)). Hedging: regression of ΔV_t on ΔH_t^i across generated scenarios. LASSO for instrument selection. PCA for covariance structure analysis.
Limitations on the work: Generative model may not capture all market dynamics. Arbitrage penalty is not zero for generated surfaces. Scenario re-weighting can reduce forecast accuracy in turbulent periods. No transaction costs in hedging experiments. Only SPX data tested. Computational cost of training GAN.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: SPX options data from OptionMetrics (Jan 2000 - Feb 2023). Training: Jan 2000 - Jun 2018. Test: Jun 2019 - Feb 2023. IV surfaces constructed using kernel smoothing. Grid: m ∈ {0.6, 0.7, ..., 1.4}, τ ∈ {1/252, 1/52, ..., 1}. VIX data from CBOE.
Evaluation Metric Used: Arbitrage penalty, tracking error statistics (mean, std, VaR), covariance structure (PCA), correlation structure.
keywords: Generative models; GenAI; scenario simulation; volatility surface; options; implied volatility.
Usage/ Benefits: VolGAN for scenario generation. Data-driven hedging via regression. Automatic instrument selection via LASSO. Arbitrage penalty for surface quality. PCA and correlation analysis.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it introduces a generative model for implied volatility surfaces that can be used for scenario generation and hedging, which is conceptually similar to my use of JEPA to learn a representation of price history. VolGAN learns a latent representation of the IV surface dynamics, which is analogous to what JEPA might learn for price history. The data-driven hedging approach using regression on generated scenarios is an alternative to RL-based hedging. The finding that VolGAN-based hedging outperforms delta and delta-vega hedging supports the value of learned representations. The automatic instrument selection via LASSO is relevant to my setting. I can use VolGAN as a baseline for scenario generation, the hedging methodology (regression on generated scenarios), and the evaluation metrics (tracking error, VaR). The paper also provides insight into what a good representation should capture (covariance structure, non-Gaussian distributions, time-varying correlations).
Challenges: Generative model may not capture all dynamics. Arbitrage penalty not zero. Scenario re-weighting can reduce forecast accuracy. No transaction costs in hedging. Only SPX data.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses arbitrage penalty from Cont and Vuletic (2023).

Paper title: What Does Deep Hedging Actually Learn? Delta Corrections, Regime Fragility, and Symbolic Distillation
Overview: This paper studies empirical deep hedging for S&P 500 index options under a local downside-shortfall reward. It moves beyond performance comparison by asking what the learned hedge does, when it fails, and whether it can be made auditable. TD3 agents are compared with daily-updated Black-Scholes delta hedge on same option episodes. In walk-forward tests from 2015 to 2023, agents usually learn a systematic delta haircut relative to Black-Scholes. The correction is explained by spot-implied-volatility co-movement and often improves accumulated reward and terminal downside variance, but it is regime-fragile: 2022 exposes losses in adverse daily states, while 2023 shows underhedging can raise ordinary variance when option P&L is spot-dominated and volatility channel is unusually weak. Symbolic regression distills neural policies into compact formulas that can be traded out of sample.
Technology stack: TD3 agents. Actor and critic: two hidden layers with 256 units each, leaky ReLU activations, Adam optimizer. Experience replay. Gaussian noise for exploration. Symbolic regression (not specified). Code available online.
Improvements: First mechanistic analysis of what deep hedging learns under local downside objective. Systematic delta haircut documentation. Regime fragility analysis. Symbolic distillation for interpretability. Connection to spot-IV co-movement.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Show empirical deep hedging under local downside objective learns systematic delta haircut relative to daily-updated Black-Scholes; (2) Connect haircut to spot, implied-volatility, and option-price co-movement; (3) Document regime fragility rather than treating outperformance as unconditional fact; (4) Use symbolic regression as policy distillation, producing compact hedge formulas and trading them out of sample; (5) Provide mechanistic explanation for when and why learned correction stops helping.
Methodology: TD3 with local downside-shortfall reward: r_{t+1} = 10(0.03 + PnL_{t+1}^{(100)} - κ|PnL_{t+1}^{(100)}|^α). PnL_{t+1} = C_{t+1} - C_t - δ_t(S_{t+1} - S_t) - cS_t|δ_t - δ_{t-1}|. Walk-forward: train on years up to Y-2, validate on Y-1, test on Y. 21-day episodes. Two-stage bootstrap: resample calendar windows then option episodes. Symbolic regression: fit correction to BS delta, Δ̂^SR = clip(Δ^BS + g(m,τ,σ), 0, 1).
Limitations on the work: Single asset (SPX options), single market. Only TD3 tested. No transaction costs in main experiments. Symbolic formulas inherit fragility. Regime dependence of results. No real-time implementation.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: S&P 500 index options from OptionsDX. 2015-2023. Option prices by mid-quotes. Risk-free rate from US Treasury. Valid test episodes: 75 in 2015 to 759 in 2022, 632 in 2023. Training: 20,000 sampled episodes per walk-forward model.
Evaluation Metric Used: Accumulated reward, mean terminal P&L, CVaR, downside variance, ordinary variance, underhedged share, delta gap.
keywords: empirical deep hedging; option hedging; reinforcement learning; delta hedging; symbolic regression; regime fragility.
Usage/ Benefits: Delta haircut analysis. Regime diagnostics (2022 reward failure, 2023 variance failure). Symbolic distillation for interpretability. Walk-forward backtest methodology. Two-stage bootstrap. Spot-IV co-movement explanation.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it provides a critical analysis of what deep hedging actually learns, which is directly aligned with my research question about whether JEPA-learned representations improve hedging. The finding that the agent learns a systematic delta haircut relative to Black-Scholes is a concrete example of what a learned representation might capture—the agent is learning to adjust the hedge based on spot-IV co-movement, which is information that a good representation should encode. The regime fragility analysis is directly applicable to my evaluation of JEPA robustness across market conditions. The symbolic distillation approach provides a method for interpretability that I could use to understand what my JEPA representation captures. The paper's methodology (walk-forward backtest, two-stage bootstrap, regime diagnostics) is directly reusable. The finding that the correction is explained by spot-IV co-movement supports my hypothesis that a representation capturing these dynamics (like JEPA) would improve hedging. I can use the TD3 baseline, the delta haircut analysis, the regime diagnostics, and the symbolic distillation methodology.
Challenges: Single asset, single market. Only TD3 tested. No transaction costs. Symbolic formulas inherit fragility. Regime dependence. No real-time implementation.
Key Proofs: None stated. Uses two-stage bootstrap for statistical significance.

Paper title: Tail-Safe Hedging: Explainable Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with a White-Box CBF-QP Safety Layer in Arbitrage-Free Markets
Overview: This paper introduces Tail-Safe, a deployability-oriented framework for derivatives hedging that unifies distributional, risk-sensitive reinforcement learning with a white-box safety layer tailored to financial constraints. The learning module combines an IQN-based distributional critic with a CVaR objective (IQN-CVaR-PPO), stabilized by a Tail-Coverage Controller that regulates quantile sampling via temperature tilting and tail-boosting to preserve effective tail mass at small α. The safety module solves a convex CBF-QP at every step, enforcing discrete-time control barrier inequalities together with a finance-specific constraint set (ellipsoidal no-trade band, box/rate limits, and a sign-consistency gate). The safety layer is explainable: it exposes active sets, tightness, rate utilization, gate scores, slack, and solver status—a self-contained audit trail aligned with model-risk governance.
Technology stack: IQN-CVaR-PPO: Implicit Quantile Networks for distributional critic, PPO with KL and entropy regularization. CBF-QP solved with OSQP. ABIDES/MockLOB for execution. SSVI→Dupire→VIX for surface generation. No code availability stated.
Improvements: First framework combining distributional RL, CVaR optimization, and white-box CBF-QP safety layer for hedging. Formal guarantees for safety, DRO, and CVaR. Telemetry-to-governance mapping. Tail-Coverage Controller for stable CVaR estimation at small α.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Tail-risk learning with stability: integrates distributional RL (IQN) and CVaR objectives with quantile-coverage controller and PPO+KL updates; (2) White-box CBF-QP safety: designs finance-specific CBF-QP enforcing NTB, box/rate, and sign-consistency gates with telemetry; (3) Robustness to shift: couples KL-regularized updates with DRO-motivated penalties; (4) Finance-grounded evaluation: builds arbitrage-free SSVI/Dupire/VIX simulator with ABIDES execution.
Methodology: IQN-CVaR-PPO: distributional critic Q_ψ(x,u;τ) approximates quantile function, CVaR objective via quantile integral, PPO with KL and entropy regularization. Tail-Coverage Controller: temperature-tilted quantile sampling p_T(τ) ∝ exp(-τ/T), tail-boost for τ ≤ α, PID controller tracks effective tail mass. CBF-QP safety layer: discrete-time CBF constraints h_i(f(x)+g(x)u) - (1-κ_iΔt)h_i(x) ≥ -ζ_i, ellipsoidal NTB e^TMe ≤ b_max, box/rate limits, sign-consistency gate g_cons(x,u) ≥ 0. QP formulation with H-metric deviation, linear trading frictions, slack penalty.
Limitations on the work: Synthetic market only (SSVI→Dupire→VIX with ABIDES/MockLOB execution). Simplified execution and microstructure. Approximation in safety-layer modeling (linearized CBF surrogates). Estimator variance and controller tuning. Trust-region and robustness assumptions. Metric coverage (CVaR at given α). Generalization across books and instruments. Governance and compliance boundaries. Computational constraints.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: SSVI→Dupire→VIX with ABIDES/MockLOB execution. Heston fallback. Stress dimensions: level/slope/curvature of SSVI, equity-vol correlation, impact strength/decay, time-to-expiry. Unified sample sizes and multiple seeds.
Evaluation Metric Used: VaR, ES/CVaR, mean, standard deviation, Sharpe, Sortino, Omega ratio, policy KL, tail coverage, active set, tightest constraint, rate utilization, gate score, slack, solver status/time.
keywords: risk-sensitive reinforcement learning, distributional RL, CVaR, trust-region methods, control barrier functions (CBFs), quadratic programming (QP), safe RL, explainable AI, deep hedging, arbitrage-free volatility.
Usage/ Benefits: IQN-CVaR-PPO architecture. Tail-Coverage Controller. CBF-QP safety layer with telemetry. Formal guarantees for safety, DRO, and CVaR. Telemetry-to-governance mapping. Ablation methodology.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is highly relevant because it provides a framework for risk-sensitive deep hedging with a white-box safety layer, which addresses my concern about robustness and interpretability of learned representations. The IQN-CVaR-PPO learning module is directly applicable to my CVaR objective. The CBF-QP safety layer provides a method for enforcing financial constraints (no-trade band, leverage limits) by construction, which I could incorporate into my hedging policy. The telemetry-to-governance mapping is useful for explainability. The formal guarantees (robust forward invariance, DRO upper bound, CVaR concentration) provide theoretical grounding. However, the paper does not use learned representations—it uses hand-crafted features (prices, Greeks, surface features). The application is to SPX-VIX hedging, not simulated Heston. I can use the IQN-CVaR-PPO architecture, the CBF-QP safety layer, the Tail-Coverage Controller, and the evaluation methodology. The paper's approach to combining distributional RL with CVaR and safety filters is directly relevant to my goal of building a robust, risk-sensitive hedging policy.
Challenges: Synthetic market only. Simplified execution. Linearized CBF surrogates. Estimator variance. Trust-region assumptions. Metric coverage. Generalization across books and instruments. Computational constraints.
Key Proofs: Theorem 1 (robust forward invariance), Proposition 1 (minimal-deviation projection), Theorem 2 (KL-DRO upper bound), Theorem 3 (CVaR concentration), Theorem 4 (CVaR trust-region improvement), Theorem 5 (feasibility persistence), Proposition 2 (negative-advantage suppression). Proofs in Appendix A.

Paper title: Risk-Sensitive Option Market Making with Arbitrage-Free eSSVI Surfaces: A Constrained RL and Stochastic Control Bridge
Overview: This paper formulates option market making as a constrained, risk-sensitive stochastic control problem in which the policy must jointly optimize trading revenues and maintain an arbitrage-free, smooth implied-volatility (IV) surface. A fully differentiable eSSVI layer is embedded inside the learning loop, enforcing static no-arbitrage (butterfly/calendar) through smoothed lattice penalties while the agent controls half-spreads, delta-hedging intensity, and structured surface deformations (state-dependent ρ-shift and ψ-scale). Executions are intensity-driven and respond monotonically to spreads and relative mispricing; tail risk is shaped with a differentiable CVaR objective via the Rockafellar-Uryasev program. Theoretically, they prove grid-consistency and convergence rates for butterfly/calendar surrogates, primal-dual grounding of learnable dual action, differentiable CVaR estimators, eSSVI wing-growth bound consistent with Lee's moment constraints, and policy-gradient validity. In simulation, the agent achieves positive adjusted P&L in most intraday segments while keeping calendar violations at numerical zero and butterfly violations at numerical floor.
Technology stack: eSSVI layer for surface parameterization. PPO with Gaussian policy (actor/critic: 2-layer MLPs, tanh activations, hidden size 64). CVaR via Rockafellar-Uryasev. Named algorithms: PPO, GAE, CMDP, eSSVI, CVaR.
Improvements: First framework integrating arbitrage-free eSSVI surface inside RL loop for option market making. Primal-dual interpretation of learnable dual action. Differentiable CVaR estimators with mixed pathwise/likelihood-ratio gradients. eSSVI wing-growth bound consistent with Lee's moment constraints.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Two-way bridge between stochastic control and deep RL: integrates arbitrage-free eSSVI surface into control loop; (2) Risk-sensitive RL with financial semantics: training objective includes CVaR alongside arbitrage and smoothness; (3) Mathematical guarantees: differentiability and Lipschitz properties of butterfly/calendar surrogates, existence of optimal stationary policies, calibration-stability, CVaR policy-gradient identity; (4) Reproducible agent-based evaluation.
Methodology: CMDP formulation: max_π E[Σγ^t r(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})] - λ_risk CVaR_q(Σγ^t ℓ(...)) subject to constraints. Action a_t = (α_t, hedge_t, ψ-scale_t, ρ-shift_t, dual_t). Reward: PNL^quote + PNL^hedge - λ_shape Shape - (λ_arb + dual) Arb - λ_cvar CVaR. eSSVI deformation: θ̃=θ, ρ̃=ρ+ρ-shift, φ̃=φ·ψ-scale. Intensity-based executions: λ_buy/sell = λ_0 w(k)[1 - σ(β(ask/bid - C*))]. Learning: warm-start + PPO with structural annealing. Dual head as learnable Lagrange multiplier.
Limitations on the work: Simulation-only (Heston fallback; ABIDES-ready but not enabled). Exogenous order flow. Static (not dynamic) arbitrage. Hedging granularity (delta only). Tail objective estimation (per-step surrogate). Warm-start introduces prior over policy class. Single-asset focus.
Datasets/Benchmarks Used: Simulated: Heston fallback (μ, κ, θ, ξ, ρ calibrated to SPX intraday variance). 8 intraday episodes of 780 decision steps. ABIDES-style sources supported but not enabled.
Evaluation Metric Used: Adjusted P&L, no-arbitrage surrogates (BF, CAL), shape regularization magnitude, tail metrics (VaR5%, CVaR5%), average spread, hedge ratio, action standard deviation.
keywords: Option market making; implied volatility surface; arbitrage-free modeling; eSSVI; SVI; risk-sensitive reinforcement learning; constrained MDP (CMDP); policy gradient; Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO); primal-dual optimization; intensity-based executions; Hawkes/point processes; delta/vega/vanna; stochastic control; agent-based simulation; neural-SDE; deep hedging.
Usage/ Benefits: eSSVI layer for arbitrage-free surface parameterization. CMDP formulation with CVaR. Primal-dual interpretation of dual action. Differentiable CVaR estimators. Interpretability of control heads. Formal guarantees for grid-consistency and CVaR gradient validity.
Why It is related To My domain: This paper is relevant because it provides a framework for integrating a differentiable arbitrage-free surface into a risk-sensitive RL loop, which is conceptually similar to my use of JEPA as a learned representation that could encode market structure. The eSSVI layer acts as a structured prior, analogous to how JEPA might provide a structured representation of price history. The CVaR objective and the primal-dual interpretation of the dual action are relevant to my risk-sensitive objectives. The interpretability of control heads (α, ψ-scale, ρ-shift, dual) provides a template for understanding what my learned representation captures. However, the application is to option market making, not option hedging, and the state is hand-crafted (surface parameters, inventory, LOB features). I can use the eSSVI layer as a baseline for surface representation, the CVaR optimization methodology, and the interpretability analysis. The formal guarantees (grid-consistency, CVaR gradient validity) are useful for validating my approach.

Key Proofs: Theorem 2 (T1: Butterfly surrogate consistency and rate), Theorem 3 (T2: Calendar surrogate consistency and rate), Theorem 4 (T3.1: Strong duality for CMDP), Theorem 5 (T3.2: Gradient alignment of learnable dual with dual ascent), Theorem 6 (T4.1: RU representation and epi-convergence), Theorem 7 (T4.2: Differentiable CVaR estimators and gradient validity), Theorem 8 (T5: Linear wing-growth bound under θφ cap), Theorem 9 (T6: Existence and boundedness of policy gradient). Propositions 4-5 (P7-P8: Monotonicity and sensitivity results). Proofs in Appendix A.

Paper title: Robust and Efficient Deep Hedging via Linearized Objective Neural Network
Overview: This paper proposes Deep Hedging with Linearized-objective Neural Network (DHLNN), a robust and generalizable framework that enhances the training procedure of deep learning models. By integrating a periodic fixed-gradient optimization method with linearized training dynamics, DHLNN stabilizes training, accelerates convergence, and improves robustness to noisy financial data. The framework incorporates trajectory-wide optimization and Black-Scholes Delta anchoring, ensuring alignment with established financial theory while maintaining flexibility to adapt to real-world market conditions. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real market data validate DHLNN's ability to achieve faster convergence, improved stability, and superior hedging performance across diverse market scenarios.
Technology stack: DHLNN: 4 hidden layers, 64 neurons each, ReLU activation. Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.001, β1=0.9, β2=0.999, ε=10^-8). Nested optimization with periodic fixed-gradient updates. No code availability stated.
Improvements: Periodic fixed-gradient optimization with linearized training dynamics. Trajectory-wide optimization. Black-Scholes Delta anchoring. Bounded Hessian and gradient change rate analysis.
Contributions to the state of Art: (1) Proposes DHLNN with periodic fixed-gradient optimization and linearized training dynamics; (2) Incorporates trajectory-wide optimization and Black-Scholes Delta anchoring; (3) Demonstrates faster convergence, improved stability, and superior hedging performance on synthetic and real market data; (4) Provides convergence and robustness analysis with bounded Hessian and gradient change rate.
Methodology: Nested optimization: outer iterations compute gradients via backpropagation, inner iterations optimize linearized objective with fixed gradients. Linearized approximation: f̂(x,w) = f(x,w^r) + ∇_w f(x,w^r)^T(w - w^r). Anchor hedge: Δ_t^l = δ_t^bs - f(x,w), Δ_t^u = δ_t^bs + f(x,w), δ_{t+1} = min{max{Δ_t^l, δ_t}, Δ_t^u}. Training: 10,000 trajectories per epoch, σ=0.1 during training, tested at σ=0.2, 0.3, 0.4. Transaction costs: 2×10^-3 to 8×10^-3.
